question.text: Two particles are launched from ground level toward each other, from two points 15 m apart. The particle at the first point moves at 10 m/s, directed 30° above the horizontal toward the second point. The particle at the second point moves at 5√2 m/s, directed 45° above the horizontal toward the first point. Do the two particles meet in the air?
conditions: both particles launched from ground level
the two launch points are 15 m apart
each particle is aimed toward the other's launch point
first particle: speed 10 m/s at 30° above horizontal
second particle: speed 5√2 m/s at 45° above horizontal

figure.description: Two points on level ground, 15 m apart. From the left point, a particle is launched toward the right point at 10 m/s, 30° above the horizontal. From the right point, a particle is launched toward the left point at 5√2 m/s, 45° above the horizontal.

solution.approach: Both particles land back on the ground at the same time because their vertical launch speeds are equal; check whether their horizontal gap has closed by that time.

steps.text: Resolve both launch velocities into horizontal and vertical parts.
The vertical speeds are equal, so both particles trace the same height-versus-time curve and land at the same instant.
Find the time at which the horizontal gap of 15 m would close, using the closing speed of the two horizontal components.
Compare the closing time with the landing time; since t_close is larger, both particles reach the ground before the horizontal gap closes, so they do not collide.

final_answer.value: No, they do not collide; both particles land at t = 1 s, before the horizontal gap (which needs about 1.10 s) closes.

common_mistakes.text: Checking only that the two particles reach the same height at the same time, without also checking that the horizontal gap has closed by then, wrongly concludes they collide.

question.text: Referring to the launch angles marked in the sketch, determine the projectile's time of flight and its range measured along the slope, with g = 10 m/s².
conditions: projectile launched from a point on an inclined surface
launch angle measured from a horizontal reference at that point
g = 10 m/s²
projectile launched toward the downhill side of the slope

figure.description: A slope rises from left to right, meeting the horizontal ground at 30° (the angle is marked at the bottom-left corner, where the slope meets the ground). From a launch point partway up the slope a dashed horizontal reference line is drawn; the velocity arrow of 20√2 m/s starts at that point and points up and to the left, that is, away from the rising slope and toward the downhill side, making 45° with the dashed horizontal line.

solution.approach: Resolve the velocity and gravity along and perpendicular to the incline. Here the velocity points over the downhill side, so it makes 45°+30° with the incline surface.

steps.text: The launch point is on the incline, with a horizontal dashed line drawn through it. The velocity makes 45° with this horizontal line but points away from the slope on the downhill side, so the projectile lands lower down the incline.
steps.why_this_step: On the downhill side the incline surface itself runs below the horizontal, so the velocity angle from the slope adds the incline angle instead of subtracting it.

steps.text: Take axes along the incline, downhill taken as positive, and perpendicular to it, away from the surface taken as positive. Resolve the initial velocity and gravity into these two directions.
steps.equation: along incline: u cos75° ; perpendicular: u sin75° ; g along incline: g sin30° ; g perpendicular: g cos30°

steps.text: The projectile returns to the incline surface when the perpendicular displacement becomes zero again. This gives the time of flight.

Range along the incline is the along-incline distance covered in time T. Gravity's along-incline part adds to this motion here, since it also points down the slope. Time of flight and range along the incline are both stated below.

common_mistakes.text: Using the angle difference 45°−30° instead of the sum 45°+30° gives T ≈ 1.69 s and R ≈ 39.04 m, which is the answer for the projectile fired up the incline, not down it.
Ignoring the incline and using the flat-ground formulas T = 2u sinθ/g and R = u² sin2θ/g gives T = 4 s and R = 80 m, missing that the ground here is sloped.

question.text: A particle travels in the xy-plane under a constant acceleration of magnitude a, always pointing along the negative y-direction. Its trajectory follows y = bx − cx², with b and c both fixed positive numbers. Work out the particle's velocity right at the coordinate origin.
conditions: acceleration of magnitude a directed along the negative y-axis
trajectory y = bx − cx², with b and c positive constants

solution.approach: Compare the given path with the standard projectile trajectory equation to read off the angle and speed of projection.

steps.text: Write the standard equation of a projectile's path for initial speed u, angle θ, and acceleration a directed along negative y.
Match this term by term with the given path.
steps.equation: y = bx − cx², so tanθ = b and a/(2u²cos²θ) = c

steps.text: Solve the second relation for the horizontal part of the initial velocity.
The velocity at the origin is the initial velocity of projection, so use u cosθ together with the angle θ from step 2 to write the full speed.
Substitute u cosθ from step 3 to state the final speed and direction; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: u = √(a(1+b²)/(2c)), directed at angle θ = tan⁻¹b above the x-axis

final_answer.value: v = √(a(1+b²)/(2c)), directed at angle θ = tan⁻¹b above the x-axis

question.text: A particle leaves the ground at 20√2 m/s, launched at 45° above the horizontal. Consider the 3 s stretch beginning at launch, that is, from t = 0 s up to t = 3 s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out the particle's change in velocity over this interval.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the size of the particle's average velocity over this interval.

conditions: projected from the ground
initial speed 20√2 m/s
angle 45° above the horizontal

solution.approach: Find the velocity at t = 3 s for the change in velocity, and the displacement at t = 3 s for the average velocity.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical parts of the initial velocity.
Find the velocity components at t = 3 s.
Subtract the initial velocity from this to get the change in velocity.
State the magnitude and direction of the change in velocity.
Find the displacement at t = 3 s and its magnitude.
Divide the displacement magnitude by the time for the average velocity; this gives the final answer.

final_answer.value: (a) change in velocity = 30 m/s, directed vertically downward; (b) average velocity ≈ 20.62 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Averaging the initial speed and the speed at t = 3 s, about (28.28 + 22.36)/2 ≈ 25.32 m/s, instead of dividing displacement by time, gives a wrong average velocity.

question.text: A projectile launches at elevation angle α above the horizontal. Viewed from the launch point, after t seconds it appears to be at elevation angle β. Determine the launch speed of the projectile.
conditions: projected at elevation angle α
observed elevation angle is β after time t, as seen from the launch point

solution.approach: The apparent elevation angle is the angle of the position vector, so its tangent equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal displacement.

steps.text: Write the horizontal and vertical displacements at time t for a projectile launched at angle α with speed u.
steps.equation: x = u cos α · t, y = u sin α · t − ½gt²

steps.text: The apparent elevation β is the angle the line from the launch point to the particle makes with the horizontal, so its tangent is y divided by x.
steps.equation: tan β = y/x = tan α − gt/(2u cos α)

steps.text: Solve this equation for u.
steps.equation: u = gt / [2 cos α (tan α − tan β)]

steps.text: Rewrite the denominator using the difference formula for sine to reach the standard form.
steps.equation: u = gt cos β / [2 sin(α − β)]

final_answer.value: u = gt cos β / [2 sin(α − β)]

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the ½ in the vertical displacement formula doubles the g t term inside the tangent equation and gives twice the correct initial velocity.

question.text: A projectile leaves the ground at a launch speed of 50 m/s, directed at 37° from the horizontal. Using g = 10 m/s², with sin 37° taken as 0.6 and cos 37° taken as 0.8, work out the projectile's velocity, its displacement, and its x–y position relative to the launch point, 2 seconds after being fired.
conditions: projectile launched from ground level (origin)
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: The projectile starts at the origin of an x-y axis system and moves at 37° above the horizontal x-axis with initial speed 50 m/s, while gravity of magnitude 10 m/s² pulls it downward.

solution.approach: Resolve the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical parts, then apply the constant horizontal velocity and accelerated vertical velocity equations at t = 2 s.

steps.text: Resolve the initial velocity into components using the given angle.
Horizontal velocity stays constant; find the vertical velocity at t = 2 s using v = u − gt.
Combine the two velocity components into the resultant velocity and its direction.
steps.equation: v = √(40²+10²) = 10√17 ≈ 41.2 m/s, at tan⁻¹(10/40) ≈ 14° above the horizontal
steps.why_this_step: The resultant speed and direction come from combining the unchanged horizontal part with the reduced vertical part.

steps.text: Find the displacement components using x = uxt and y = uyt − ½gt², then their magnitude.
Collect the three results asked for.
steps.equation: velocity ≈ 41.2 m/s at ≈14° above horizontal; displacement ≈ 89.4 m; coordinates (80 m, 40 m)

final_answer.value: Velocity ≈ 41.2 m/s at about 14° above the horizontal; displacement ≈ 89.4 m; coordinates (80 m, 40 m).

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the speed stays 50 m/s since gravity does not change the horizontal part, without recomputing the vertical component 30 − 10×2 = 10 m/s; this gives 50 m/s instead of about 41.2 m/s.
Finding the vertical displacement as uy×t = 30×2 = 60 m and leaving out the −½gt² term, giving 60 m instead of 40 m.

question.text: A stationary mortar launches a bomb upward at 53° to the horizontal, leaving the muzzle at 80 ms⁻¹. At the instant of firing, a tank begins moving straight toward the mortar across flat ground at a steady 5 m/s. Taking g = 10 ms⁻², find how far apart the mortar and tank must initially be for the bomb to strike the tank.
conditions: mortar is fixed in place
tank moves on flat, level ground
tank moves directly toward the mortar starting at the instant of firing
bomb must strike the tank
g = 10 ms⁻²

solution.approach: The bomb's time of flight and range depend only on its own speed and angle; the tank must be at the landing point exactly when the bomb arrives there.

steps.text: Find the time of flight of the bomb using the vertical launch speed and gravity.
Find the horizontal range of the bomb using the horizontal launch speed and the time of flight.
In this time the tank moves toward the mortar at its own constant speed.
For a hit, the tank's distance from the mortar must fall from the initial separation D to exactly the bomb's range R in this same time.
Solve for D and compare with the printed values; 678.4 m equals none of the first three options, so the fourth option is correct.
steps.equation: D = 614.4 + 64 = 678.4 m → option (d), None of these

final_answer.value: 678.4 m (None of these)

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sin 53° and cos 53° (using 0.6 and 0.8 the wrong way round) keeps the range the same but shortens the flight time, giving 662.4 m.
Taking the separation as equal to the bomb's range alone, ignoring that the tank also moves toward the mortar, gives 614.4 m, which matches no option.

question.text: A trainer launches a baseball to a teammate, sending it off at 20 m/s at 45° above horizontal. The instant the throw happens, the teammate is standing 50 m away. Using g = 10 m/s², determine the running speed and direction the teammate needs so the catch happens exactly at the height the ball started from.
conditions: ball thrown by coach to player
player starts 50 m from coach at the moment of throw
player must catch ball at the same height as release
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Find where the ball lands using the range formula, then find the speed needed to close the remaining gap in the time of flight.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical parts of the throw's initial velocity.
Find the time of flight, since the ball returns to the height it was released at.
Find how far the ball travels horizontally in that time.
The player starts 50 m away and must reach the point 40 m away where the ball lands, so find the distance to close.
Divide this distance by the time of flight for the running speed; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: v = 10/(2√2) = 5√2/2 ≈ 3.54 m/s, running toward the trainer

final_answer.value: about 3.54 m/s, running toward the trainer

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the full initial separation of 50 m by the time of flight, instead of the 10 m gap left to close, gives a wrong speed of about 17.68 m/s.

question.text: In the diagram, a projectile is launched from point O with an initial speed of 20√2 m/s, directed 45° above the horizontal, up a slope that rises at 37° to the horizontal. The projectile comes down on the slope's surface at point P.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine how long the projectile stays in the air before landing on the slope at P.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the distance OP measured along the slope, from the launch point O to the landing point P.

conditions: particle launched from point O
launch speed is 20√2 m/s
launch angle is 45° above the horizontal
the slope rises at 37° to the horizontal
particle lands on the slope at point P
Q is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from P onto the horizontal through O

figure.description: O is the launch point at the origin. The velocity vector, of magnitude 20√2 m/s, points up and to the right, making a 45° angle with the horizontal line OQ. A second line from O, representing the slope, rises at 37° to the same horizontal and reaches point P, where the projectile lands (a dotted vertical line drops from P down to Q on the horizontal). Reference x and y axes are shown beside the figure.

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical position as functions of time, then find where the path meets the incline's line through O, y = x tan37°.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity.
Write the horizontal and vertical positions as functions of time, using g = 10 m/s².
The incline rises at 37° from O, so P lies where the vertical position equals the horizontal position times tan37°.
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
Find x at this time, then divide by cos37° to get the distance along the incline. Restating both parts: the time of flight is 1 s and the range OP is 25 m.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 1 s, (b) OP = 25 m

common_mistakes.text: Using the equation for a particle landing below the launch point instead of above it, which gives t = 7 s and OP = 175 m.

question.text: An object is released moving only horizontally from a tower's top. It lands on the ground 3 seconds later, striking it at 45° to the horizontal. Using g = 9.8 m/s², calculate the tower's height and the horizontal launch speed of the object.
conditions: object released horizontally from tower top
lands after 3 s at 45° to the horizontal
g = 9.8 m/s²

solution.approach: Use the 45° landing angle to link the vertical and horizontal velocity components, then get the height from the time of fall.

steps.text: Find the vertical velocity built up in 3 s of fall.
At a 45° landing angle the horizontal and vertical components are equal, since tan45° = 1, so the projection speed equals this vertical component.
Find the height using the vertical-fall formula for the same 3 s.
Collect both results.

final_answer.value: Height of tower = 44.1 m, speed of projection = 29.4 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Computing the height as h = u×t = 29.4×3 = 88.2 m instead of h = ½gt², missing the one-half factor and getting exactly double the correct height.

question.text: A particle is launched horizontally at 50 ms⁻¹ from a plane tilted 30° to the horizontal. With g = 10 ms⁻², determine the distance travelled along the slope from the launch point to where the particle lands.
conditions: fired horizontally, not along the slope
inclined plane makes 30° with the horizontal
g = 10 ms⁻²

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical positions as functions of time, find when the vertical drop matches the incline's slope, then convert that point's horizontal distance to distance along the incline.

steps.text: Take the launch point as the origin. The particle moves horizontally at constant speed and falls under gravity.
The particle lands on the incline when the vertical drop equals the horizontal distance times the incline's slope.
Cancel one factor of t and solve for the landing time.
Find the horizontal distance at this time, then divide by cos30° to get the distance measured along the incline.
steps.equation: x = ut = 500/√3 m, range along incline = x/cos30° = (500/√3)/(√3/2) = 1000/3 m

common_mistakes.text: Using t = 2u/g, the flat-ground time-of-flight formula, instead of the incline formula 2u tan30°/g, and reporting the horizontal distance ut directly as the final range gives 500 m.

question.text: Someone kicks a ball upward from level ground. When the ball is 9.1 m up, an instrument records its velocity as v = 7.6î + 6.1ĵ, in metres per second, with î along the horizontal and ĵ pointing up. Approximate values are acceptable.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: What is the greatest height the ball reaches?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: How far along the ground does the ball go before it comes down?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Just before the ball hits the ground, what is the size of its velocity?

parts.label: d
parts.asks: Just before the ball hits the ground, what is the direction of its velocity?

conditions: ball shot from ground level
at height 9.1 m the velocity is v = 7.6î + 6.1ĵ m/s
î is the horizontal direction, ĵ is the upward direction
answers may be approximate

solution.approach: The horizontal speed stays fixed through the flight; use it with the vertical speed and height at the point to rebuild the launch speed and motion, g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.text: The extra height gained above the given point, before the vertical speed drops to zero, comes from the vertical speed there.
Add this to the given height to get the maximum height reached.
Find the vertical launch speed by treating the given point as reached after falling from the peak, or equivalently rising from the ground.
Find the total time of flight and the horizontal range, using the constant horizontal speed.

Just before landing, the vertical speed has the same size as the launch value but points downward; combine it with the constant horizontal speed for the landing speed and its direction below the horizontal.
steps.equation: v_land = √(7.6² + 14.7²) ≈ 16.5 m/s, at tan⁻¹(14.7/7.6) ≈ 63° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: (a) H ≈ 11.0 m, (b) R ≈ 22.8 m, (c) speed ≈ 16.5 m/s, (d) direction ≈ 63° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Taking the given height of 9.1 m directly as the maximum height, since the vertical speed there is nonzero, ignoring that the ball rises further before it stops going up.

question.text: A particle is launched from the bottom of an incline that rises at 30° to the horizontal. Its launch velocity, of magnitude u = 10 m/s, is directed 30° above the incline surface itself. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the particle's speed at the moment it lands back on the incline, at point A.
conditions: incline makes 30° with the horizontal
launch speed u = 10 m/s
launch direction makes 30° with the incline surface
g = 10 m/s²
particle lands on the incline at point A

figure.description: An inclined plane rises at 30° from a point O on the ground. A particle is launched from O at 10 m/s, its velocity making a 30° angle with the incline surface, and it follows a curved path back down to land on the incline at point A.

solution.approach: Work in axes along and perpendicular to the incline, where gravity splits into two components; find the time the particle returns to the incline, then the velocity components there.

steps.text: Resolve the launch velocity along and perpendicular to the incline, using the 30° angle between the velocity and the incline.
Resolve gravity along and perpendicular to the incline, using the 30° angle of the incline with the horizontal.
steps.equation: g∥ = g sin30° = 5 m/s², g⊥ = g cos30° = 5√3 m/s²

steps.text: Find the time to return to the incline surface, where the perpendicular displacement is again zero.
Find the along-incline and perpendicular velocity components at this time.
Combine the two components to get the speed at A.

final_answer.value: speed at A = 10√3/3 m/s ≈ 5.77 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that gravity also has a component along the incline, and keeping the along-incline speed unchanged at 5√3 m/s, gives a wrong speed of exactly 10 m/s.

question.text: In the diagram, a projectile is launched from point O with speed 20√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal. The incline through O slopes downward at 37° to the horizontal, and the projectile comes down on this incline at point P.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine how long the projectile is in the air before it lands on the sloped surface at P.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the distance OP, measured along the slope, from the launch point O to the landing point P.

conditions: particle launched from point O
launch speed is 20√2 m/s
launch angle is 45° above the horizontal
the incline slopes downward from O at 37° to the horizontal
particle lands on the incline at P

figure.description: The particle leaves O with velocity 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. The slope through O runs downward at 37° to the horizontal, both close to O and at its lower end. The particle's curved path rises then falls, meeting the slope at point P, below and to the side of O. A right-angled construction with a vertical segment from O and a horizontal segment to P marks the drop and horizontal shift used to locate P.

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical position as functions of time, then find where the path meets the incline's line through O, y = −x tan37°.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity, taking the horizontal direction in which the incline descends as positive x.
Write the horizontal and vertical positions as functions of time, using g = 10 m/s².
The incline falls away below O at 37° in this direction, so P lies where the vertical position equals minus the horizontal position times tan37°.
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
Find x at this time, then divide by cos37° to get the distance along the incline. Restating both parts: the time of flight is 7 s and the range OP is 175 m.

common_mistakes.text: Using the equation for a particle landing above the launch point instead of below it, which gives t = 1 s and OP = 25 m.

question.text: A projectile is launched with speed u directed perpendicular to an inclined surface that makes angle θ with the horizontal ground. Obtain a formula for the distance R, measured along the slope, from the launch point to where the projectile lands.
conditions: launch velocity u points perpendicular to the slope's surface
slope makes angle θ with the horizontal

figure.description: A projectile launches from the top of an inclined slope, with initial velocity u perpendicular to the slope's surface. The slope makes angle θ with the horizontal. The projectile arcs through the air and lands back on the slope, a distance R (measured along the slope) from the launch point.

solution.approach: Resolve motion along axes parallel and perpendicular to the incline; the perpendicular motion gives the time to land back on the slope, and the parallel motion gives the distance R.

steps.text: Take axes along the slope and perpendicular to it. Along the slope gravity contributes g sinθ with no initial velocity; perpendicular to the slope gravity contributes g cosθ opposing the initial velocity u.
steps.equation: a∥ = g sinθ, a⊥ = −g cosθ, u⊥ = u, u∥ = 0

steps.text: The projectile lands back on the slope when the perpendicular displacement returns to zero.
steps.equation: u t − ½g cosθ t² = 0 ⟹ t = 2u/(g cosθ)

steps.text: The distance along the slope at that time is the parallel displacement.
steps.equation: R = ½g sinθ t² = ½g sinθ × [2u/(g cosθ)]²

steps.text: Simplify to reach the expression for R.

final_answer.value: R = 2u² sinθ / (g cos²θ)

common_mistakes.text: Using t = 2u/g instead of t = 2u/(g cosθ) ignores that gravity's component perpendicular to the slope is g cosθ, not g, and gives a smaller value of R.

question.text: Two particles are launched at the same instant, moving horizontally, from two different points on a riverbank that sit at some height above the water. Particle 1 has initial speed v₁ = 5 m/s and particle 2 has initial speed v₂ = 7.5 m/s. Both particles land in the water simultaneously. The first particle lands at a horizontal distance s = 10 m from the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find how long each particle remains airborne before hitting the water.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the height of the riverbank above the water surface.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Work out where the second particle lands in the water, measured from the bank.

conditions: thrown horizontally, simultaneously, from two points on a riverbank at some height above the water surface
both particles land in the water at the same time

solution.approach: Both particles fall from the same height for the same time; the first particle's range gives that time, which then gives the height and the second particle's landing point.

steps.text: Find the time of flight from the first particle's horizontal speed and its landing distance.
Since both particles are in the air for the same time and start from the same height, use free fall from rest to find that height.
The second particle travels horizontally at its own constant speed for the same time to find where it lands.
State the three results together.
steps.equation: (a) t = 2 s, (b) h = 19.6 m, (c) x₂ = 15 m from the bank

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 s, (b) h = 19.6 m, (c) second particle lands 15 m from the bank

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the ½ in h = ½gt² gives h = 9.8 × 2² = 39.2 m, twice the correct 19.6 m.

question.text: Two slopes OA and OB, tilted at 30° and 60° to the horizontal ground respectively, meet each other at point O, as illustrated. A particle is launched from point P with speed u = 10√3 m/s along a direction perpendicular to slope OA, and it strikes slope OB perpendicularly at point Q. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The duration of the particle's flight.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The speed at which the particle hits plane OB.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: How far above point O is point P located (call this vertical height h).

parts.label: d
parts.asks: The distance PQ.

conditions: slope OA is inclined at 30° to the horizontal
slope OB is inclined at 60° to the horizontal
the two slopes meet at point O
particle launched from P with speed 10√3 m/s, perpendicular to slope OA
particle strikes slope OB perpendicularly at point Q
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: Two inclined lines meet at O on a horizontal ground line: OA rises to the upper left at 30° to the ground, OB rises to the upper right at 60° to the ground. Point P lies on OA, at height h above O. At P, the velocity u is drawn perpendicular to OA. Point Q lies on OB, with a right-angle mark showing the velocity there is perpendicular to OB. Tilted reference axes are shown near B, aligned along OB and OA.

solution.approach: Set up horizontal-vertical coordinates, place P using its height above O, then use the perpendicular-landing condition on OB together with OB's line equation.

steps.text: Resolve the launch velocity, which is perpendicular to the 30° incline OA, into horizontal and vertical parts.
Write P's coordinates using its height h above O, since P lies on the 30° incline.
Write the velocity components at time t; the horizontal part stays fixed and the vertical part changes under gravity.
Landing perpendicular to the 60° incline OB fixes the ratio of the velocity components at Q.
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
The speed at Q combines the two components (part b).
Use the position at t = 2 s together with Q lying on OB (y = √3 x) to solve for h (part c).
Find P and Q and take the distance between them. Restating every part: time of flight 2 s, speed at Q 10 m/s, height h of P is 5 m, distance PQ is 20 m.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 s, (b) v = 10 m/s (perpendicular to OB), (c) h = 5 m, (d) PQ = 20 m

common_mistakes.text: Using the 30° angle in OB's line equation instead of the 60° angle, which gives a wrong height h = 0 m for part (c).

concept_tags: resolving velocity perpendicular to a plane

question.text: A passenger sitting inside a train releases a stone from their hand while the train keeps moving at a steady speed.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Describe the shape of the path the stone follows as seen by that same passenger.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Describe the shape of the path the stone follows as seen by someone standing still on the ground.

conditions: stone is dropped (released with zero relative velocity) by a passenger inside a moving train
train moves at constant velocity

solution.approach: The stone keeps the train's horizontal velocity, so the passenger and the man on the ground see two different paths for the same drop.

steps.text: The passenger keeps moving forward with the train at the same horizontal velocity as the stone, so relative to the passenger the stone has no horizontal velocity.
Relative to the passenger, the stone only has a vertical acceleration g acting on it, so the passenger sees the stone fall straight down.
The man on the ground sees the stone keep the train's horizontal velocity while it also picks up vertical velocity from gravity.
A constant horizontal velocity combined with a vertical acceleration traces a curved path, the same shape as a horizontal projectile.
So the passenger sees a straight vertical line, and the man on the ground sees a parabolic path.
steps.why_this_step: The two observers are in different frames: one moves with the stone's horizontal motion, the other does not.

final_answer.value: (a) A straight vertical line, as seen by the passenger. (b) A parabola, as seen by the man on the ground.

common_mistakes.text: Thinking the man on the ground also sees the stone fall straight down, forgetting the stone keeps the train's horizontal velocity after release.
Thinking the passenger sees a curved path, forgetting the passenger is also moving forward with the train at the stone's own horizontal speed.

question.text: From the top of a 25 m tall tower, a particle is thrown with a speed of 20√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal. Work out how long it takes to reach the ground, how far horizontally from the base of the tower it lands, and its velocity at the moment it lands.
conditions: projected from a tower of height 25 m
î marks the horizontal direction and ĵ marks the vertically upward direction

solution.approach: Split the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical parts, then use the vertical motion equation to find when the particle falls 25 m below the launch point.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical parts of the initial velocity.
Take upward as positive and write the vertical position from the top of the tower; it equals −25 m when the particle reaches the ground.
Substitute the values and solve the resulting quadratic equation for t.
steps.why_this_step: The other root, t = −1 s, is before the particle is projected, so it is rejected.

steps.text: Find the horizontal distance from the foot of the tower using the constant horizontal velocity.
Find the velocity components at t = 5 s.
steps.equation: vx = 20 m/s, vy = uy − gt = 20 − 50 = −30 m/s

steps.text: Combine the components for the speed and direction at collision; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: speed = √(20² + 30²) = 10√13 ≈ 36.06 m/s, about 56.3° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: t = 5 s, horizontal distance = 100 m, velocity ≈ 36.06 m/s at about 56.3° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the tower height and using the ground level time of flight formula T = 2uy/g gives t = 4 s and distance 80 m, both wrong since the particle falls an extra 25 m.

question.text: A bullet launched at 30° to the horizontal lands 3.0 km from where it was fired. If the launch angle is changed while everything else about the shot is kept the same, is it possible to strike a target sitting 5.0 km away? The bullet leaves the barrel at a constant speed, and air drag can be ignored.
conditions: launch angle can be changed
muzzle (launch) speed stays constant
air resistance is neglected

solution.approach: Find the maximum possible range at this fixed muzzle speed and compare it with the target distance.

steps.text: Write the range formula and use the given range at 30° to relate it to the muzzle speed.
The maximum range for a fixed speed occurs at 45°, where sin2θ = 1, so the maximum range equals u²/g.
Compute this value.
Compare this maximum with the target distance to answer the question; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: 5.0 km is greater than 3.46 km, so no angle can reach the target

final_answer.value: No. The maximum range at this muzzle speed is about 3.46 km, less than 5.0 km, so no angle of projection can hit the target.

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the given range by sin30° instead of sin60° gives a wrong maximum range of 6.0 km, wrongly suggesting the target can be hit.

question.text: A projectile is aimed at a target that lies in the same horizontal level as the launch point. Launched at elevation α, it lands a cm short of the target; launched at elevation β with the same launch speed, it overshoots the target by b cm. Prove that the elevation angle that would hit the target exactly is ½ sin⁻¹[(b sin 2α + a sin 2β)/(a + b)].
conditions: target lies in the horizontal plane through the point of projection
launch speed is the same for both elevation angles

solution.approach: Both shots share the same range formula and the same unknown target range R; eliminating u and R between the two elevation equations gives the elevation that hits the mark.

steps.text: Let R be the true distance to the mark. At elevation α the shot falls short by a, so the range achieved is R − a; at elevation β it goes b beyond, so the range achieved is R + b.
steps.equation: u² sin2α/g = R − a, u² sin2β/g = R + b

steps.text: Divide the two equations to eliminate u, then solve for R in terms of a, b, α and β.
The correct elevation γ gives range R with the same speed, so its sine of double angle equals gR divided by u². Use u² = g(R − a)/sin2α from the first equation.
Substitute R from the earlier step and simplify the fraction to reach the stated result.
steps.equation: sin2γ = (b sin2α + a sin2β)/(a + b), so γ = ½ sin⁻¹[(b sin2α + a sin2β)/(a+b)]

final_answer.value: γ = ½ sin⁻¹[(b sin2α + a sin2β)/(a+b)]

common_mistakes.text: Swapping a and b in the final formula, writing (a sin2α + b sin2β)/(a+b) instead, gives a different value for a general pair of angles and distances.

question.text: A pair of complementary projection angles have flight durations T₁ and T₂. Which expression correctly gives the projectile's range R?
conditions: T₁ and T₂ are flight durations for a pair of complementary projection angles

solution.approach: Write the times of flight for the two complementary angles, multiply them, and compare with the range formula for the same speed.

steps.text: Write the times of flight for the two complementary angles θ and (90° − θ), both launched at the same speed u.
Multiply the two times of flight.
Write the range formula and substitute u²sin2θ from it into the T₁T₂ expression.
steps.equation: R = u²sin2θ/g, so u²sin2θ = Rg, T₁T₂ = 2Rg/g² = 2R/g

steps.text: Rearrange for the range in terms of T₁ and T₂.

final_answer.value: R = ½ gT₁T₂

common_mistakes.text: Writing the time of flight without the factor of 2, as T = u sinθ/g, gives R = 2gT₁T₂ instead.

question.text: A ball leaves a thrower's hand moving exactly horizontally, starting from a height of 100 m over the ground, with a horizontal launch speed of 20 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out how long the ball takes before it lands.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out how far horizontally the ball travels before landing.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Work out the landing velocity, giving both its size and its direction.

conditions: ball thrown horizontally
launched from a point 100 m above the ground

solution.approach: Use the vertical fall to find the time, the constant horizontal speed for the distance, and combine both velocity parts at landing.

steps.text: Find the time to fall 100 m from rest in the vertical direction.
Find the horizontal distance travelled using the constant horizontal speed.
Find the vertical velocity at landing.
Combine the horizontal and vertical parts for the speed and direction at landing; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: v = √(20² + (20√5)²) = 20√6 ≈ 48.99 m/s, about 65.9° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: (a) t ≈ 4.47 s; (b) x ≈ 89.44 m; (c) v ≈ 48.99 m/s at about 65.9° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the factor ½ in the fall equation and using t = √(h/g) instead of √(2h/g) gives a wrong time of about 3.16 s.

question.text: For a projectile, find the launch angle at which its horizontal range equals its maximum height.
conditions: horizontal range equals maximum height

solution.approach: Write range and maximum height in terms of the projection angle, set them equal, and solve for the angle.

steps.text: Write the standard range and maximum-height formulas.
Set R equal to H and expand sin2θ.
Divide through by sinθ, which is nonzero for a real projectile, and solve for θ.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the maximum-height formula without the factor 2 in the denominator, H = u²sin²θ/g, which gives tanθ = 2 and a different wrong angle of about 63.4°.

question.text: A small ball leaves point A at t = 0, launched at 60 m/s at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, find the two instants t₁ and t₂ at which the ball's velocity is directed 45° from the horizontal x-axis.
conditions: projected from point A at t = 0
air resistance neglected

solution.approach: The horizontal speed stays fixed at u cos60°; the velocity is at 45° to the horizontal when the vertical speed equals the horizontal speed, once rising and once falling.

steps.text: Write the constant horizontal component of velocity.
Write the vertical component of velocity as a function of time.
The velocity makes 45° with the horizontal when the size of the vertical component equals the horizontal component.
Solve for the rising case, where the vertical component is still upward.
Solve for the falling case, where the vertical component now points downward.

final_answer.value: t₁ ≈ 2.2 s (rising) and t₂ ≈ 8.2 s (falling)

common_mistakes.text: Solving only the rising case and stopping at t ≈ 2.2 s misses the second moment, after the peak, when the velocity again makes 45° with the horizontal.
Mistaking the question for the total time of flight and computing 2u sin60°/g gives about 10.4 s, which is neither correct time.

question.text: Assertion: We describe projectile motion as two-dimensional even though the motion actually happens within three-dimensional space. Reason: Even in three-dimensional space, the motion stays confined to a single flat plane.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: projectile motion physically occurs in three-dimensional space
the motion stays within a single plane

solution.approach: Projectile motion happens in three-dimensional space, but the path always lies inside one fixed plane set by the launch velocity and gravity.

steps.text: Gravity always points straight down, and the initial velocity has some fixed direction in space.
These two directions together fix a single plane that contains the whole path, since nothing pushes the particle sideways out of that plane.
Because the entire trajectory stays inside this one plane, only two coordinates are needed to describe the motion at any instant.
This is exactly why projectile motion is called two dimensional even though it happens somewhere in three-dimensional space, so the Assertion is true and the Reason correctly explains it.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason states the geometric fact — motion confined to one plane — that directly gives the Assertion its two-dimensional description.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Thinking that because projectile motion happens in three-dimensional space, the Reason about it lying in one plane must be false.
Agreeing both statements are true but doubting that the Reason actually explains the Assertion, when it directly does.

question.text: For a fixed launch speed u, two different projection angles can give the same horizontal range. Prove that adding together the maximum heights reached for these two angles gives a result that does not depend on which of the two angles was used.
conditions: two different launch angles yield equal horizontal range for the same launch speed u

solution.approach: For a given range, the two projection angles are complementary; write the maximum height for each and add them.

steps.text: Two angles giving the same range are θ and (90°−θ); write the maximum height for each.
Add the two heights and use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
steps.why_this_step: The angle θ cancels out completely, leaving only u and g, so the sum does not depend on which pair of complementary angles is used.

final_answer.value: H₁ + H₂ = u²/(2g), a constant that does not depend on θ.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two range formulas instead of the two height formulas, getting R₁+R₂ = 2u²sin2θ/g, which still depends on θ and does not show the required result.

question.text: Two particles, A and B, are launched at the same instant from two points on level ground. Particle A leaves the ground at speed 20 m/s, directed at an unknown angle θ above the line joining the two points, toward B. Particle B leaves the ground moving straight up at 10 m/s. The two particles meet in the air half a second after launch.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the angle θ.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the horizontal distance x between the two launch points.

conditions: A and B launched simultaneously
A's speed is 20 m/s, directed at angle θ above the ground toward B
B's speed is 10 m/s, directed straight upward
the particles collide in the air 1/2 s after launch

figure.description: Two points, A and B, lie on level ground a horizontal distance x apart. From A, a particle is launched toward B at 20 m/s, at an unknown angle θ above the ground. From B, a particle is launched straight upward at 10 m/s.

solution.approach: Both particles start on the ground and fall under the same gravity, so matching their heights at the collision time cancels the fall term and fixes the angle directly.

steps.text: Write the height above the ground of each particle as a function of time.
steps.equation: y_A(t) = v_A sinθ·t − ½gt², y_B(t) = v_B·t − ½gt²

steps.text: Set the two heights equal at the collision time; the −½gt² term cancels on both sides.
steps.equation: v_A sinθ·t = v_B·t → v_A sinθ = v_B

steps.text: Substitute the given speeds to find the angle.
Use the given collision time to find A's horizontal distance covered, which equals the separation x since B does not move horizontally.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the fall term for particle A only, instead of letting it cancel for both particles, gives a wrong angle of about 22.0° and a wrong distance of about 9.27 m.

question.text: A body is thrown upward so that its position vector, in metres, changes with time t (in seconds) as r = 3t î + (4t − 5t²)ĵ. Find the time at which its y-coordinate becomes zero, and the x-coordinate of the body at that time.
conditions: position vector r = {3t î + (4t − 5t²)ĵ} m
t measured in seconds

solution.approach: Read the y-coordinate directly from the given position vector, set it to zero, and solve for the non-zero time; then use that time in the x-coordinate.

steps.text: Read the y-coordinate as a function of time from the position vector.
Set the y-coordinate to zero and factor.
Take the non-zero root, since t = 0 is the starting instant.
Substitute this time into the x-coordinate.

common_mistakes.text: Setting the rate of change of y to zero, instead of y itself, finds the time of the highest point (0.4 s) and gives a wrong x-coordinate of 1.2 m.

question.text: A lift is moving upward, accelerating at 1 m/s². At the moment its speed reaches 2 m/s, a stone is thrown from the lift's floor, its speed relative to the lift being 2 m/s, launched upward at 30° elevation.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out how long the stone takes before it lands back on the lift's floor.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Draw the trajectory the stone follows, as seen by someone standing outside the lift.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Suppose instead the lift accelerates downward at a rate equal to g. Describe how the stone's motion would then differ.

conditions: lift accelerating upward at 1 m/s²
stone launched from the lift's floor with velocity given relative to the lift
elevation angle of launch is 30° relative to the lift

solution.approach: Inside the accelerating elevator the stone feels an increased effective gravity g + a, so its relative flight time follows the usual projectile formula with that effective value.

steps.text: Find the stone's vertical velocity component relative to the elevator at launch.
Inside the upward-accelerating elevator, the effective downward acceleration felt by the stone relative to the elevator is g plus the elevator's own acceleration.
steps.equation: g_eff = g + a = 10 + 1 = 11 m/s² (taking g = 10 m/s²)

steps.text: Use the usual projectile time-of-flight formula with this effective gravity to find when the stone returns to the elevator floor.
steps.equation: t = 2v_rel/g_eff = 2×1/11 = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s, with g = 9.8 m/s², g_eff = 10.8 m/s² and t ≈ 0.185 s

steps.text: For an observer outside the elevator, the stone's initial velocity is the elevator's velocity plus the stone's velocity relative to the elevator. After release the stone moves under ordinary gravity g alone, so it follows a normal parabolic path; the elevator floor, still accelerating upward, rises to meet the stone.
steps.equation: vₓ = 2cos30° ≈ 1.73 m/s, v_y = 2 + 2sin30° = 3 m/s, both measured from the ground

steps.text: If the elevator instead accelerates downward at g, it is in free fall, so the effective gravity felt inside it becomes zero.
State all three results together.
steps.equation: (a) t = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s taking g = 10 m/s² (≈ 0.185 s with g = 9.8 m/s²), (b) a parabola in the ground frame with initial velocity 1.73 m/s horizontal and 3 m/s upward, (c) with downward acceleration g the effective gravity inside is zero, so relative to the elevator the stone moves in a straight line at constant velocity and never returns to the floor

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 sin30°·2/(g + 1) = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s taking g = 10 m/s² (≈ 0.185 s with g = 9.8 m/s²), (b) a parabola in the ground frame with initial velocity 1.73 m/s horizontal and 3 m/s upward, while the elevator floor, still accelerating upward, rises to meet the stone, (c) with downward acceleration g the elevator is in free fall, so relative to it the stone moves in a straight line at constant velocity and never returns to the floor

common_mistakes.text: Using ordinary gravity g instead of the effective gravity g + a for the time in part (a) gives 0.2 s instead of the correct 0.18 s.

question.text: Launched from the ground at 50 m/s, a particle makes an angle of 37° with the horizontal. Taking sin 37° = 3/5, determine both its velocity and its displacement 2 seconds after launch.
conditions: projected from ground level

solution.approach: Find the horizontal and vertical velocity components at launch, then use the equations of motion at t = 2 s for both velocity and displacement.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity, using g = 10 m/s².
Find the velocity components at t = 2 s; the horizontal component stays fixed.
Combine the components to get the velocity at t = 2 s.
Find the horizontal and vertical displacement at t = 2 s.
Combine the displacements to get the net displacement at t = 2 s. Restating both parts: the velocity is 10√17 m/s and the displacement is 40√5 m.

final_answer.value: velocity v = 40î + 10ĵ m/s (magnitude 10√17 m/s ≈ 41.2 m/s); displacement s = 80î + 40ĵ m (magnitude 40√5 m ≈ 89.4 m)

common_mistakes.text: Using the initial vertical velocity 30 m/s unchanged at t = 2 s instead of subtracting gt, giving a wrong speed of 50 m/s.
Leaving out the −½gt² term in the vertical displacement, giving y = 60 m and a wrong net displacement of 100 m.

question.text: A particle undergoes projectile motion, launched at speed u at an angle θ above the horizontal. What is its average velocity between the launch point and the highest point of its path?
conditions: projection speed is u
angle of projection from horizontal is θ

solution.approach: Average velocity is displacement over time. Find the horizontal and vertical displacement to the highest point and divide by the time taken to reach it.

steps.text: The time to reach the highest point is when the vertical velocity becomes zero.
Find the horizontal and vertical displacement reached in this time.
steps.equation: x = u cosθ · t = u² sinθ cosθ / g ; y = u² sin²θ / (2g)

steps.text: Average velocity is this displacement divided by the time taken, giving its horizontal and vertical parts separately.
steps.equation: vx = x / t = u cosθ ; vy = y / t = u sinθ / 2
steps.why_this_step: Dividing each displacement part by the same time gives the two parts of the average velocity vector.

steps.text: The size of the average velocity combines both parts, matching option (b).

common_mistakes.text: Taking the velocity at the highest point, which is purely horizontal with size u cosθ, and mistaking it for the average velocity between the start and the highest point gives option (a).

Combining the initial speed u with the horizontal speed at the top, u cosθ, as if they were two perpendicular sides and halving the result gives option (d) instead of averaging the velocity parts properly.

question.text: From the foot of a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal, a particle is launched at 40 m/s, directed 60° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the particle's speed at the moment its velocity is directed parallel to the slope.
conditions: launched from the bottom of an incline
incline angle 30° with horizontal
launch speed 40 m/s
launch angle 60° with horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: The velocity is parallel to the incline when its direction from the horizontal equals the incline angle; the constant horizontal component then fixes the speed directly.

steps.text: Write the constant horizontal component and the time-varying vertical component of velocity.
The velocity is parallel to the incline when its angle from the horizontal equals the incline's angle of 30°.
Solve for the time at which this holds.
At this angle, the horizontal component and the speed are related through the cosine of 30°, giving the speed directly.

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sine and cosine in the horizontal component of the launch velocity gives a wrong horizontal speed and a wrong final speed of exactly 40 m/s.

question.text: From the top of a 70 m tower a ball is thrown at 50 ms⁻¹, 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 ms⁻², after how many seconds does it reach the ground?
conditions: thrown from the top of a tower of height 70 m
thrown upward at 30° above the horizontal
g = 10 ms⁻²

solution.approach: Write the vertical displacement as a function of time, set it to minus the tower height since the ball lands below the launch point, and solve the quadratic for time.

steps.text: Find the vertical component of the launch velocity.
Write the vertical displacement equation, taking upward as positive, with the ground 70 m below the launch point.
Rearrange into standard quadratic form and simplify.
Solve the quadratic. Only the positive root is a physical time.

final_answer.value: 7 s

common_mistakes.text: Taking the magnitude of the rejected negative root instead of discarding it gives 2 s.
Ignoring the tower height and finding only the time to return to the launch height, 2u_y/g, gives 5 s.

question.text: A projectile leaves a cliff top moving purely horizontally at 98 m/s; the cliff is 490 m tall.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: How long does the projectile take before it lands?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: How far from the base of the cliff does the projectile land?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: With what velocity (magnitude and direction) does the projectile strike the ground? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

conditions: fired horizontally from the top of a hill
hill height = 490 m
g = 9.8 m/s²

figure.description: The projectile starts at the top of the cliff moving horizontally, follows a curving downward path, and lands at a point on the ground level with the foot of the cliff; at landing its velocity has a horizontal component and a vertical component making an angle with the horizontal.

solution.approach: Split the motion into a constant horizontal part and a vertical free-fall part timed by the fall height, then combine components for each part asked.

steps.text: Find the time to fall the 490 m height from a purely horizontal launch.
Use the constant horizontal velocity and this time to get the horizontal distance.
Find the vertical velocity built up by gravity at landing, then combine it with the unchanged horizontal velocity.
steps.equation: vy = gt = 9.8×10 = 98 m/s, v = √(98²+98²) = 98√2 ≈ 138.6 m/s, β = 45° below horizontal
steps.why_this_step: vx equals vy here, so the resultant velocity direction bisects the two, giving exactly 45°.

steps.text: Collect all three results.
steps.equation: (a) t = 10 s, (b) 980 m, (c) 98√2 ≈ 138.6 m/s at 45° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: (a) t = 10 s, (b) 980 m, (c) 98√2 ≈ 138.6 m/s at 45° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Using t = h/g = 490/9.8 = 50 s instead of t = √(2h/g), forgetting the square root and the factor of 2 in the time-of-fall formula.

question.text: Two balls, A and B, are thrown at the same instant from the tops of two towers standing distance d apart. Ball A is thrown from the shorter tower, of height 10 m, at 10√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal toward the other tower. Ball B is thrown from the taller tower, of height 20 m, horizontally toward the first tower at 10 m/s. The two balls meet while both are still in the air. Find d.
conditions: particle A projected from a 10 m tower at 10√2 m/s, 45° above horizontal, toward the other tower
particle B projected from a 20 m tower horizontally toward A at 10 m/s
both particles launched at the same instant
the particles collide while airborne

figure.description: Two vertical towers stand on level ground, distance d apart. The left tower is 10 m tall; from its top, particle A is launched at 45° above the horizontal at 10√2 m/s, aimed toward the right tower. The right tower is 20 m tall; from its top, particle B is launched horizontally at 10 m/s, aimed toward the left tower.

solution.approach: Write the height of each particle above the ground as a function of time and find when the heights match; use that time to find the horizontal gap to close.

steps.text: Resolve particle A's launch velocity into horizontal and vertical parts.
Write the height of each particle above the ground as a function of time, measuring from its own tower.
Set the two heights equal and solve for the collision time; the −5t² term cancels on both sides.
At this time, A has moved a horizontal distance 10t toward B, and B has moved 10t toward A; together they cover the full gap d.

final_answer.value: d = 20 m

common_mistakes.text: Using only ball A's horizontal motion for the gap gives d = 10 m; adding ball B's 10 m motion toward A in the same time gives the correct d = 20 m.

question.text: A ball is launched at a speed of 20 m/s, at whatever angle to the horizontal gives it the greatest possible horizontal range. What is its speed when it is at the topmost point of its path?
conditions: launch speed is 20 m/s
launch angle chosen for maximum range

solution.approach: Maximum range happens at 45°, and the horizontal velocity component stays constant through the flight, so it equals the speed at the highest point.

steps.text: The range is maximum when the angle of projection is 45°.
At the highest point the vertical velocity component is zero, so the speed there equals the horizontal component, which never changes.
Substitute u = 20 ms⁻¹ and θ = 45° and compute the value, which rounds to the nearest printed option.

final_answer.value: 14 ms⁻¹

common_mistakes.text: Wrongly assuming the maximum-range angle is 60° instead of 45° and computing 20 × cos 60° gives 10 ms⁻¹.

question.text: Someone stands at the top of a sloping hill and throws a stone purely horizontally, giving it speed v₀. Using an x-y axis system with its origin at the throwing point, work out the x and y coordinates of the spot on the hillside where the stone eventually lands.
conditions: stone thrown horizontally from the hill top with speed v₀
origin of coordinates placed at the point of projection
x-axis horizontal, y-axis vertical
hill surface (incline) makes angle θ with the horizontal

figure.description: The hill's top is at the origin (0,0) of an x-y axis system, with the x-axis horizontal (pointing in the direction of throw) and the y-axis vertical. The stone is thrown horizontally with speed v₀ along the positive x direction from the origin. The hillside slopes downward from the origin at angle θ below the horizontal x-axis, and the stone's curved path meets this sloped hillside at a point (x, y), with y measured as negative below the origin.

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical distances travelled as functions of time, then find where the path meets the sloped hill surface.

steps.text: Use the axes given in the question: origin at the launch point, x horizontal along v₀, y vertical and positive upward. Then x(t) = v₀t and y(t) = −½gt².
The hill surface is the straight line y = −x tanθ through the origin; set the path equal to this line and solve for t.
Substitute this time back into x(t) and y(t) to get the landing coordinates.

final_answer.value: The stone lands at (x, y) = (2v₀²tanθ/g, −2v₀²tan²θ/g); the negative sign shows the landing point lies below the launch point, as in the figure.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the hill's equation with the angle on the wrong side, y = −x cotθ instead of y = −x tanθ, which replaces every tanθ in the landing time and coordinates by cotθ.

question.text: Assertion: Whenever the acceleration of a particle does not change, the only path it can trace is a parabola. Reason: The trajectory in projectile motion is a parabola because, near the ground, the acceleration is treated as unchanging.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: acceleration is taken as constant when the heights involved are small (as in projectile motion)

solution.approach: Constant acceleration alone does not force a curved path; a velocity launched along the acceleration direction gives a straight line instead.

steps.text: Consider a particle given an initial velocity pointing along the same line as the constant acceleration, for example thrown straight up under gravity.
Its sideways coordinate never changes, since there is no sideways velocity and no sideways acceleration.
So this particle moves along a straight vertical line, not a parabola, even though its acceleration is constant the whole time.
This counterexample shows the Assertion is false: constant acceleration does not by itself force a parabolic path.

The Reason is a separate, true statement — projectile motion is parabolic because its acceleration is treated as constant at low heights — but the Reason being true does not make the Assertion true, so the Assertion is false and the Reason is true.
steps.why_this_step: This combination matches the option for a false Assertion with a true Reason.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Believing constant acceleration always produces a curved path, missing the case where the initial velocity points along the acceleration.
Judging both statements true without checking whether a straight-line counterexample exists under constant acceleration.

question.text: Two particles start from the same point above a tower and, at that instant, move horizontally in opposite directions with speeds v₁ = 3 m/s and v₂ = 4 m/s, falling freely under gravity g afterward. Find how far apart they are at the moment their two velocity vectors are perpendicular to each other.
conditions: both particles start from the same point
gravitational acceleration is g
initial velocities are horizontal and in opposite directions
asks for the instant when the velocity vectors are mutually perpendicular

solution.approach: Write each particle's velocity vector as a function of time, set the dot product to zero for perpendicularity, then find the horizontal separation at that time, since both fall equally.

steps.text: Write the velocity vectors of the two particles in one set of axes, rightward and upward positive; the first particle moves rightward and the second leftward.
Set the dot product of the two velocity vectors to zero for perpendicularity.
Solve for the time at which the vectors are perpendicular.
Since both particles fall the same vertical distance from the same height, the distance between them is purely horizontal, equal to the sum of their horizontal speeds times this time.
steps.equation: distance = (v₁ + v₂)t = (v₁ + v₂)√(v₁v₂)/g = 7×2√3/g = 14√3/g m; with g = 10 m/s², d = 14√3/10 = 7√3/5 ≈ 2.42 m; with g = 9.8 m/s², d ≈ 2.47 m ≈ 2.5 m

final_answer.value: distance = 14√3/g m: ≈ 2.42 m with g = 10 m/s² (t = 2√3/g ≈ 0.35 s), ≈ 2.47 m ≈ 2.5 m with g = 9.8 m/s² (t ≈ 0.35 s)

common_mistakes.text: Using t = (v₁ + v₂)/g in place of t = √(v₁v₂)/g gives a wrong time of 0.7 s and a wrong distance of 4.9 m (with g = 10 m/s²).

question.text: A projectile launched at angle θ, with a certain speed, covers a horizontal range that equals half the maximum range obtainable at that same speed. What is the angle θ?
conditions: range at angle θ is half the maximum range
same launch speed used for both ranges

solution.approach: Set the range formula at angle θ equal to half the maximum range and solve for θ.

steps.text: Write the range at angle θ and the maximum range, both at the same speed u.
steps.equation: R(θ) = u²sin2θ / g, R_max = u² / g (at θ = 45°)

steps.text: Set the range at θ equal to half the maximum range.
Cancel u²/g from both sides and solve for 2θ, then θ.
steps.equation: sin2θ = ½, so 2θ = 30° or 150°, θ = 15° or 75°; of these only 15° is among the options

common_mistakes.text: Taking 2θ = 30° but then forgetting to divide by 2 gives θ = 30°.
Writing 2θ = 120° instead of 30° or 150°, by confusing sin 120° (which is √3/2) with ½, gives θ = 60°.

question.text: A particle is launched at 20 m/s, at 60° above the horizontal. Using g = 10 m/s², find the time at which the particle's speed has dropped to half of its initial value.
conditions: launch speed 20 m/s
launch angle 60° above horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: The horizontal component of velocity never changes and equals u cos60° = u/2, so the total speed equals half the initial speed only when the vertical component vanishes.

steps.text: Find the constant horizontal component of velocity.
Note that the total speed at any time is at least vₓ, since v = √(vₓ² + v_y²), and equals vₓ exactly when v_y = 0.
Since the target speed u/2 equals this minimum, find the time at which v_y = 0, which is the time to reach the highest point.
Solve for that time.

common_mistakes.text: Setting the vertical component itself equal to half the initial speed, instead of the total speed, gives v_y = u/2 and a wrong time of about 0.73 s.

question.text: Demonstrate that a projectile passes through the same height at two separate instants, and prove algebraically that adding those two times together gives exactly the total time of flight.
conditions: projectile reaches the same height at two different times

solution.approach: Write the height reached at time t as a quadratic equation, and use the sum-of-roots relation to show the two times at that height add to the time of flight.

steps.text: Write the vertical displacement at time t as a quadratic equation in t, for a chosen height y₀.
This quadratic has two positive roots t₁ and t₂ for any height below the maximum, since the same height is crossed once going up and once coming down.
Add the two roots; the square-root terms cancel and the sum matches the standard time-of-flight formula.
steps.why_this_step: The sum of the roots of at² + bt + c = 0 is −b/a, which here gives 2u sinθ/g directly, without needing the individual root values.

final_answer.value: t₁ + t₂ = 2u sinθ/g = T, the time of flight.

common_mistakes.text: Multiplying the two roots instead of adding them, getting t₁×t₂ = 2y₀/g, a quantity unrelated to the time of flight.

question.text: Three separate particles are each launched from the top of the same 40 m tall tower, one per case, with different launch conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: First case: the particle is launched at 45° above the horizontal, up and away from the tower, with speed 20√2 m/s. Find the landing time and the horizontal landing distance from the tower's base.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Second case: the particle is launched horizontally with speed 20 m/s. Find the landing time and the horizontal landing distance from the tower's base.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Third case: the particle is launched at 45° below the horizontal, downward and away from the tower, with speed 20√2 m/s. Find the landing time and the horizontal landing distance from the tower's base.

conditions: three particles, each launched from the top of the same 40 m tower in a separate case
case i: launched at 45° above horizontal, away from the tower
case ii: launched horizontally
case iii: launched at 45° below horizontal, away from the tower

figure.description: A 40 m tall tower is shown three times, once per case. In case i a particle leaves the top of the tower at 45° above the horizontal, moving up and away from the tower, with speed 20√2 m/s. In case ii a particle leaves the top horizontally with speed 20 m/s. In case iii a particle leaves the top at 45° below the horizontal, moving down and away from the tower, with speed 20√2 m/s. An x-y axis convention (x horizontal, y vertical) is shown alongside.

solution.approach: Resolve each throw into horizontal and vertical components and solve the vertical drop equation for each case, taking g = 10 m/s² since it is not stated.

steps.text: Resolve each launch velocity into components; the 20√2 m/s at 45° throws split into equal horizontal and vertical parts, while case (ii) is purely horizontal.
steps.equation: 20√2×cos45° = 20√2×sin45° = 20 m/s (cases i and iii); case ii: vx = 20 m/s, vy0 = 0

steps.text: Case (i), thrown upward and away: solve the vertical drop equation for a net fall of 40 m below the launch point.
Case (ii), thrown horizontally: solve the same drop equation with zero initial vertical velocity.
Case (iii), thrown downward and away: solve the drop equation with initial vertical velocity 20 m/s downward.
Collect all three cases.

final_answer.value: (i) t ≈ 5.46 s, distance ≈ 109.3 m; (ii) t ≈ 2.83 s, distance ≈ 56.6 m; (iii) t ≈ 1.46 s, distance ≈ 29.3 m (using g = 10 m/s²)

common_mistakes.text: Using the horizontal-only time from case (ii), t = 2√2 ≈ 2.83 s, for case (i) and case (iii) too, ignoring that their initial vertical velocity is not zero.

question.text: One particle is launched straight upward at 20 m/s. At the same instant, a second particle is launched at 20√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal, with g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of the first particle as measured relative to the second particle.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the initial velocity of the first particle as measured relative to the second particle.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the separation between the two particles 2 s after launch.

conditions: both particles launched at the same instant
first particle projected vertically upward at 20 m/s
second particle projected at 20√2 m/s at 45° to the horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Both particles fall under the same gravity, so their relative acceleration is zero and the gap between them grows at a constant rate.

steps.text: Write each particle's initial velocity in horizontal and vertical components.
Both particles are in free flight under gravity alone, so each has the same downward acceleration.
The acceleration of the first particle relative to the second is the difference of the two accelerations.
steps.equation: a₁ − a₂ = (0, 0) m/s², so part (a) is 0

steps.text: The initial velocity of the first particle relative to the second is the difference of the two initial velocities.
steps.equation: u₁ − u₂ = (0−20, 20−20) = (−20, 0) m/s, magnitude 20 m/s, so part (b) is 20 m/s

steps.text: Since the relative acceleration is zero, the relative velocity stays (−20, 0) m/s for the whole flight, so the separation after any time t is this relative velocity times t.
At t = 2 s the separation along this constant relative velocity gives the distance between the particles.
steps.equation: Δr(2) = 20 × 2 = 40 m, so part (c) is 40 m
steps.why_this_step: With zero relative acceleration the two particles move apart in a straight line at a fixed relative speed.

final_answer.value: (a) 0 (the relative acceleration is zero), (b) 20 m/s horizontally, directed opposite to the second particle's horizontal motion, i.e. (−20, 0) m/s, (c) 40 m

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the second particle has a different acceleration because part of its velocity is horizontal, which wrongly makes the relative acceleration nonzero.
Using only one particle's own displacement after 2 s instead of the relative displacement between the two particles to find the separation.

question.text: From a point O at the foot of a slope that rises at 30° to the horizontal, a particle is thrown with speed 10 m/s along a direction making 30° with the slope surface (that is, 60° above the horizontal). It lands on the slope at a point A. Take g = 10 m/s². At the instant it reaches A, find the component of its velocity perpendicular to the slope surface.
conditions: slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal
launch speed 10 m/s at 30° to the slope surface
g = 10 m/s²
the particle lands on the slope at A

solution.approach: In axes along and perpendicular to the incline, the perpendicular motion is like a simple up-and-down toss, so the perpendicular speed at landing equals the launch value, reversed in direction.

steps.text: Resolve the launch velocity perpendicular to the incline, using the 30° angle between the velocity and the incline.
steps.equation: u⊥ = 10sin30° = 5 m/s, away from the incline

steps.text: The perpendicular motion is decelerated uniformly by g⊥ = g cos30° and returns to zero perpendicular displacement, exactly like a ball tossed straight up and caught at the same level.
So the perpendicular component at A has the same size as at launch, but points into the incline.
steps.equation: v⊥ = 5 m/s, directed into the plane

final_answer.value: 5 m/s, directed into the inclined plane

question.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the motion of a projectile?

options.1: The acceleration stays the same, in both magnitude and direction, at every point of the path.
options.2: The acceleration is uniform throughout the path, except that at the topmost point the object moves with constant velocity.
options.3: At no point of the flight is the acceleration vector perpendicular to the velocity vector.

solution.approach: Gravity keeps acting with the same constant value throughout the flight, including at the highest point, which rules out the other statements.

steps.text: Through the whole flight, the only acceleration acting on the projectile is gravity, which stays constant in magnitude and direction.
Even at the highest point, where the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, gravity still acts, so the acceleration there is the same nonzero constant value as everywhere else.
So the motion is uniformly accelerated at every point of the path, including the top, which rules out the statement that velocity becomes constant there.

At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal while the acceleration is purely vertical, so their dot product is zero there, meaning acceleration and velocity are perpendicular at that instant, which rules out the statement that they are never perpendicular.
The only statement that holds throughout the flight is that projectile motion is uniformly accelerated everywhere.

final_answer.value: It is uniformly accelerated everywhere

common_mistakes.text: Thinking that zero vertical velocity at the highest point means zero acceleration there, mistaking momentarily zero velocity for constant velocity.
Assuming acceleration and velocity can never be perpendicular in projectile motion, missing that this happens exactly at the highest point.

question.text: From the top of a tower, two particles are launched at the same instant, moving horizontally but away from each other — one at 10 m/s, the other at 20 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s², work out after how long their velocity directions become perpendicular to each other.
conditions: projected horizontally from a tower
particles move in opposite horizontal directions
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Write each particle's velocity vector including gravity's effect on the vertical component, then set the dot product to zero.

steps.text: Write the velocity of each particle at time t, taking their horizontal launch directions as opposite and both falling under gravity.
The vectors are mutually perpendicular when their dot product is zero.
Simplify this equation.
Solve for the time.

common_mistakes.text: Solving t² = 2 by dividing 200 by 100 and stopping there, giving t = 2 s instead of taking the square root to get t = √2 s.

question.text: Assertion: When the time of flight of a projectile is doubled, its maximum height increases to four times its earlier value. Reason: For a projectile, the maximum height H is proportional to the square of the time of flight T, that is H ∝ T².

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: projectile motion
maximum height H is proportional to the square of the time of flight T (H ∝ T²)

solution.approach: Time of flight and maximum height both come from the same vertical launch speed, so height is proportional to the square of the time of flight.

steps.text: Write time of flight and maximum height in terms of the vertical component of the launch velocity.
Solve the time of flight equation for the vertical launch speed and substitute it into the height formula.
With g fixed, this shows the maximum height is proportional to the square of the time of flight.
Doubling the time of flight squares that factor of two inside the height formula.

So doubling the time of flight makes the maximum height four times as large, and the Reason (H ∝ T²) is exactly the relation that gives this result, so both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming H ∝ T² is false because height is usually written in terms of launch speed and angle rather than directly in terms of time of flight.
Accepting both statements as true but treating H ∝ T² as a side fact rather than the direct algebraic reason for the fourfold increase.

question.text: At the highest point of its path, a projectile's speed equals √(2/5) times its speed at a height equal to half the maximum height reached. Work out the angle at which it was projected.
conditions: speed at the greatest height is compared with the speed at half the greatest height
ratio of the two speeds is √(2/5)
standard projectile motion under gravity

solution.approach: Write the speed at the top and at half the maximum height in terms of u and θ, then use the given ratio to solve for θ.

steps.text: At the greatest height, the vertical velocity is zero, so the speed is only the horizontal component.
At half the greatest height H/2, use the vertical velocity-height relation, with H the maximum height.
Substitute H into the vertical velocity expression and simplify.
The speed at half height combines both components.
Apply the given ratio v_top = √(2/5) v_half and square both sides.
Solve for the angle of projection.

common_mistakes.text: Using half the time to reach the top instead of half the maximum height, which gives tan²θ = 6 and θ ≈ 67.8° instead of 60°.

question.text: A particle is launched from ground level at speed u, making angle α with the horizontal. Determine its average velocity for the entire duration — from the instant of launch to the instant it lands back on the ground.
conditions: projected from the ground
launch speed u at angle α with the horizontal
considered over the full flight until it lands again

solution.approach: Average velocity is total displacement over total time; since the particle lands at the same height, only the horizontal part of the displacement survives.

steps.text: Write the time of flight and the range for a particle projected from and landing on the ground.
