Over this interval the particle starts and ends at the same height, so the net vertical displacement is zero and the horizontal range is the only displacement.
Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time.
Substitute R and T and simplify.
steps.equation: v_avg = (u²sin2α/g) divided by (2u sinα/g) = (2u²sinα cosα)/(2u sinα) = u cosα

steps.text: State the result; this is the final answer.

final_answer.value: u cosα, directed horizontally (equal to the constant horizontal part of the initial velocity)

question.text: Assertion: For a projectile, if you pick any two positions along its path with velocities v₁, v₂ occurring at times t₁, t₂, the ratio (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) always works out to the same value. Reason: This ratio is the average acceleration, and it stays fixed because the acceleration of the projectile does not change.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: v₁, v₂ are the velocities at two positions during projectile motion
t₁, t₂ are the corresponding times

solution.approach: The ratio of the change in velocity to the change in time between any two instants is by definition the average acceleration, which equals the constant acceleration in projectile motion.

steps.text: Write the definition of average acceleration between two instants of time.
In projectile motion the acceleration is constant and equal to g downward at every instant, with no other force acting.
Since the instantaneous acceleration never changes, the average acceleration between any two chosen instants must also equal this same constant value.
So the ratio (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) always equals g downward, whichever two positions are chosen, and the Reason correctly names this ratio as the average acceleration, which is why it stays constant.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason states the definition that directly explains why the Assertion holds for any pair of instants.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the ratio changes with the chosen positions because velocity itself keeps changing throughout the flight.
Accepting both statements as true but treating the Reason as a separate fact rather than the definition that directly explains the Assertion.

question.text: A particle leaves the ground with initial speed u = 20√2 m/s at an angle θ = 45° to the horizontal, taken as the x-axis.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the horizontal range R, the maximum height H, and the total time of flight T.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the particle's velocity 1 second after launch.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the particle's velocity at the moment it lands back on the ground, that is, on the x-axis.

conditions: projected from the ground
initial speed u = 20√2 m/s
angle θ = 45° to the horizontal
the ground is taken as the x-axis

figure.description: A small sketch shows the x-y coordinate axes with the initial velocity vector u drawn from the origin, making angle θ with the horizontal x-axis.

solution.approach: Find the horizontal and vertical velocity parts, then use the range, height and time formulas and the velocity equation at each time asked.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical parts of the initial velocity.
Find the time of flight, maximum height and range using g = 10 m/s².
steps.equation: T = 2uy/g = 4 s, H = uy²/(2g) = 20 m, R = ux T = 80 m

steps.text: Find the velocity components 1 s after projection.
steps.equation: vx = 20 m/s, vy = uy − g(1) = 10 m/s

steps.text: Combine these for the speed and direction at t = 1 s.
steps.equation: v = √(20² + 10²) = 10√5 ≈ 22.36 m/s, about 26.6° above the horizontal

steps.text: Find the velocity components at the time of collision, t = T = 4 s.
Combine these for the speed and direction at landing; this gives the final answer.

final_answer.value: (a) R = 80 m, H = 20 m, T = 4 s; (b) v ≈ 22.36 m/s at about 26.6° above the horizontal at t = 1 s; (c) v ≈ 28.28 m/s at 45° below the horizontal at landing

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the factor 2 in the height formula and using H = uy²/g gives 40 m instead of the correct 20 m.

question.text: Assertion: In the x-y plane a particle moves with an unchanging acceleration whose two components aₓ and aᵧ are both non-zero. Such a particle can never trace a parabola. Reason: A projectile has no acceleration along the horizontal.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: acceleration is constant in the x-y plane
neither the x-component nor the y-component of acceleration is zero

solution.approach: A parabolic path only needs a constant acceleration that is not along the velocity; it does not need the acceleration's components to vanish in one particular pair of axes.

steps.text: Choose x and y axes tilted away from the direction of the constant acceleration, so both its components aₓ and aᵧ are nonzero in these axes.
Give the particle an initial velocity that is not along the acceleration direction, and follow its path using these tilted axes.
The traced path is still the same physical parabola it would be in axes aligned with the acceleration; only its equation looks different when written in the tilted axes.
So a particle can still have a parabolic path even when neither aₓ nor aᵧ is zero, which makes the Assertion false.
The Reason is a true statement about projectile motion described in axes aligned with gravity, but a true Reason does not make a false Assertion true.
steps.why_this_step: The Assertion is about the shape of the path, which does not depend on the choice of axes.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the shape of the path depends on which axes are chosen, so nonzero aₓ and aᵧ are mistaken for proof that the path cannot be a parabola.
Treating the Assertion as true because it resembles the usual projectile description, without checking it against a tilted choice of axes.

question.text: Two objects are launched with identical initial speeds, one at an angle θ above the horizontal and the other at an angle (90° − θ) above the horizontal. What is the ratio of the maximum heights they reach?
conditions: both objects launched with the same initial speed
launch angles are θ and (90° − θ) measured from the horizontal

solution.approach: Maximum height depends on sin squared of the angle of projection, so write it for both angles and compare.

steps.text: Write the maximum height formula for a body launched at angle θ with speed u.
Write the maximum height for the second body, launched at angle (90° − θ) with the same speed.
Divide the two heights. The u² and 2g cancel, leaving the ratio of the squared sine and cosine terms.

final_answer.value: sin²θ : cos²θ

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the two complementary angles always give equal maximum height, like they give equal range, gives the ratio 1 : 1.
Writing the ratio with sine and cosine to the first power instead of squared gives sin θ : cos θ.

question.text: A ball is thrown from ground level. It just clears a wall of height 3 m standing 6 m from the launch point, and lands on the ground 18 m beyond the wall. Find the angle at which the ball was thrown.
conditions: thrown from ground level
wall height 3 m
wall is 6 m from the point of projection
ball lands 18 m beyond the wall
ball just clears the wall

solution.approach: Use the trajectory equation in terms of range; the total range is the sum of the two given distances, and the wall height fixes a point on the path.

steps.text: Find the total horizontal range, which is the distance to the wall plus the distance from the wall to the landing point.
Write the trajectory equation in the form that uses the range directly.
Substitute the wall's position and height into this equation.
Solve for the angle of projection.

common_mistakes.text: Using only the distance beyond the wall as the range, instead of adding the distance to the wall, gives tanθ = 3/4 and a wrong angle of about 36.9°.

question.text: A ball leaves the ground moving at 60° above the horizontal; its kinetic energy at launch is K. At a later instant its velocity is directed at 30° above the horizontal. What is the kinetic energy at that instant?
conditions: projected at 60° to the horizontal
kinetic energy at projection is K
later velocity makes 30° with the horizontal

solution.approach: The horizontal velocity component stays constant through the flight, so use it to link the speed at the two angles, then compare kinetic energies.

steps.text: Write the initial kinetic energy and the horizontal velocity component, which stays the same throughout the flight.
At the point where the velocity makes 30° with the horizontal, the horizontal component of the new speed v equals the same constant horizontal component.
Solve for v, then form the kinetic energy ratio using v² and u².
So the kinetic energy at the new angle is one third of the original.

common_mistakes.text: Directly computing the new speed as v = u cos30° instead of solving for it from the constant horizontal component gives K' = K cos²30° = 3K/4.

question.text: A train travels along a straight track at 30 ms⁻¹. Someone on the train throws a ball at 30 ms⁻¹, directed at 45° above the horizontal and perpendicular to the train's motion. Calculate the separation between the spot on the train where the ball left and the spot on the ground where it lands.
conditions: train moves at constant 30 ms⁻¹ along the track
ball thrown perpendicular to the train's direction of motion
ball thrown at 45° above the horizontal

solution.approach: The ball keeps the train's velocity along the track, so only the sideways and vertical motion from the throw separate it from the point on the train where it launched.

steps.text: Split the thrown velocity, given perpendicular to the train's motion at 45° above horizontal, into its sideways and vertical parts.
steps.equation: v_sideways = 30 cos45°, v_up = 30 sin45°, both equal 30/√2 ms⁻¹

steps.text: Along the track, the ball moves with the train's own speed the whole time, so it stays directly alongside the point on the train where it was thrown; that separation stays zero.
Find the time of flight from the vertical motion, using g = 10 ms⁻² and landing back at the same height it was thrown from.
The only separation from the launch point on the train is the sideways displacement, since the along-track and vertical net displacements are both zero.

question.text: At a point 45 m above the ground, a projectile's velocity is v = (30î + 40ĵ) m/s, where î and ĵ are unit vectors along the horizontal and vertical directions respectively. Work out the projectile's initial velocity, its total time in the air, the greatest height it reaches, and the horizontal distance it covers.
conditions: projectile's velocity at a height of 45 m above the ground is v = (30î + 40ĵ) m/s
î and ĵ are unit vectors along the horizontal and vertical directions respectively
standard projectile motion under gravity, launched from ground level

figure.description: A parabolic path starts at origin O and rises then falls back to the horizontal ground far to the right. Near the launch point, the initial velocity's horizontal and vertical components are marked. Higher up on the curve, at a point 45 m above the ground, the velocity components at that point are marked, the horizontal one equal in length to the launch value and the vertical one shorter.

solution.approach: Use the vertical velocity-height equation between the launch point and height 45 m to find the initial vertical component, then get every other quantity from it.

steps.text: The horizontal velocity component stays constant throughout the flight.
Relate the vertical velocity at height 45 m to the initial vertical velocity, using g = 10 m/s².
Solve for the initial vertical velocity, taking the positive root since the particle is still rising at this height.
The initial velocity is the vector sum of the two components.
Find the time of flight and the maximum height from the initial vertical component.
Find the horizontal range using the time of flight. Restating every quantity: initial velocity 30î + 50ĵ m/s (10√34 m/s), time of flight 10 s, maximum height 125 m, range 300 m.

final_answer.value: initial velocity u = 30î + 50ĵ m/s (magnitude 10√34 m/s ≈ 58.3 m/s); time of flight T = 10 s; maximum height H = 125 m; horizontal range R = 300 m

common_mistakes.text: Treating the given vertical velocity 40 m/s at height 45 m as the initial vertical velocity, which gives a wrong time of flight of 8 s and a wrong maximum height of 80 m.

question.text: A projectile is launched from one corner of a horizontal base, just skims past the top vertex of a triangle, and comes down at the base's far corner. Taking α and β as the two base angles and θ as the projection angle, show that tan θ equals tan α plus tan β.
conditions: particle launched from one end of a horizontal base of a triangle
particle grazes (just touches) the opposite vertex of the triangle during flight
particle lands at the other end of the same horizontal base
α and β are the two base angles of the triangle
θ is the angle of projection

figure.description: The trajectory is drawn from origin O, rising and falling back to the horizontal X-axis at range R. A point A on the curve marks the vertex grazed by the projectile, at horizontal distance x from O and height y above the axis. At O, the launch angle θ and the angle α between line OA and the axis are marked. At the landing point, the angle β between the line from A to that point and the axis is marked. The horizontal distance from the foot of A to the landing point is R − x.

solution.approach: Write the trajectory using the range R, then read off tanα and tanβ from the vertex point A and add them.

steps.text: Rewrite the standard trajectory equation using the range R, since R = u²sin2θ/g gives g/(2u²cos²θ) = tanθ/R.
At the vertex A(x, y), the slope of the line OA gives α.
The slope of the line from A to the landing point at (R, 0) gives β.
Substitute the trajectory equation into these two slope expressions.
steps.equation: tanα = tanθ(R − x)/R, tanβ = x tanθ/R

steps.text: Add the two results; the R terms cancel, giving the required identity.
steps.equation: tanα + tanβ = tanθ[(R − x) + x]/R = tanθ

final_answer.value: tanθ = tanα + tanβ (proved)

common_mistakes.text: Assuming A is the highest point of the path and using x = R/2, which only checks the identity for that special case, not for a general point A.

question.text: Particles A and B are launched at the same instant, both moving in a single vertical plane, starting from the positions and launch angles given in the figure. At some later time t, the two particles meet each other while still airborne. State two equations that must both hold for this in-air collision to occur.
conditions: A and B launched simultaneously into one common vertical plane
starting positions and launch angles for A and B are as given in the figure
the particles meet in the air at time t

figure.description: A graph with horizontal axis x (m) and vertical axis y (m). Particle A starts at (x = 10 m, y = 10 m) and is launched with speed u₁ at angle θ₁ above the horizontal, heading up and to the right, toward B's side. Particle B starts at (x = 30 m, y = 20 m) and is launched with speed u₂ at angle θ₂ above the horizontal, heading up and to the left, toward A's side.

solution.approach: For the particles to collide, their horizontal positions must match and their vertical positions must match at the same instant t, since both fall under the same gravity.

steps.text: Write the position of each particle at time t using its own launch point, speed and angle. A moves up and to the right, B moves up and to the left.
steps.equation: x_A = 10 + u₁cosθ₁·t, y_A = 10 + u₁sinθ₁·t − ½gt²; x_B = 30 − u₂cosθ₂·t, y_B = 20 + u₂sinθ₂·t − ½gt²

steps.text: For a collision at time t, both coordinates must be equal at that instant.
In the vertical equation the −½gt² term is the same for both particles, so it cancels, leaving a simple linear equation.
The horizontal equation gives the second necessary condition.

final_answer.value: t(u₁cosθ₁ + u₂cosθ₂) = 20 and t(u₁sinθ₁ − u₂sinθ₂) = 10

question.text: A particle is launched with speed u, directed at angle θ above the horizontal. Determine at what time its velocity becomes perpendicular to the velocity it had at launch.
conditions: particle undergoes projectile motion under gravity g
later velocity is perpendicular to the launch velocity

figure.description: The particle starts at the origin moving along direction θ above the horizontal ground with speed u; at some later instant its velocity vector points in a direction making a right angle with the original launch direction, as the particle follows a curved (parabolic) path under gravity.

solution.approach: Set up velocity components at time t, and require zero component along the initial velocity direction, since that is what perpendicularity to it means.

steps.text: Write the velocity components at time t using the projection angle θ.
steps.equation: vx = u cosθ (constant), vy = u sinθ − gt

steps.text: The velocity is perpendicular to the initial velocity u when their dot product is zero.
steps.equation: v·u = (u cosθ)(u cosθ) + (u sinθ − gt)(u sinθ) = 0

steps.text: Expand and simplify, then solve for t.
steps.equation: u²cos²θ + u²sin²θ − ugt sinθ = 0 ⇒ u² = ugt sinθ ⇒ t = u/(g sinθ)
steps.why_this_step: This is the instant the component of velocity along the original direction has fallen to zero, leaving only the perpendicular component.

final_answer.value: t = u/(g sinθ)

common_mistakes.text: Using the time to reach maximum height, t = u sinθ/g, mistaking it for the perpendicular-velocity condition; the two times are different unless θ = 90°.

question.text: A particle is launched from level ground with speed u at an angle α above the horizontal and comes back down to the ground. Over the whole flight, from the moment of launch until it lands, what is the change in its velocity?
conditions: launched from ground level
the interval is the whole flight, launch to landing

solution.approach: Change in velocity is the vector difference between the velocity just before landing and the velocity at projection.

steps.text: Write the initial velocity components, with the horizontal direction as x and vertically upward as y.
steps.equation: ux = u cosα, uy = u sinα

steps.text: By the symmetry of projectile motion the particle returns to the same height with the same speed, with the horizontal part unchanged and the vertical part reversed.
Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, component by component.
State the magnitude and direction of the change; this is the final answer.

final_answer.value: 2u sinα, directed vertically downward

question.text: Particle A is launched with initial speed 60 m/s, at 30° above the horizontal. At the same moment, particle B is launched from a point 100 m away from A, moving in the reverse horizontal sense, with initial speed 50 m/s. The two particles meet each other while still airborne. Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: What launch angle α, measured above the horizontal, must particle B use?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: At what time do the two particles meet?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: What is the straight-line distance from A's launch point to the point P where they meet?

conditions: particle A projected at 60 m/s at 30° to horizontal
particle B projected simultaneously in the opposite horizontal direction at 50 m/s
B starts from a point 100 m from A
particles collide in air
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: Particle A starts at point A moving up and toward B at 60 m/s, 30° above the horizontal ground; particle B starts at point B, 100 m away along the same ground line, moving up and toward A at 50 m/s, at angle α above the horizontal; their curved paths cross at a point above the ground between A and B.

solution.approach: Both particles fall with the same acceleration, so equal vertical velocity components keep them at the same height; use that for α, then match horizontal positions for time and distance.

steps.text: Both particles start at the same height with the same downward acceleration g, so they stay at equal heights at every instant only if their initial vertical velocity components are equal.
steps.equation: uA sin30° = uB sinα ⇒ 60×0.5 = 50 sinα ⇒ sinα = 0.6 ⇒ α = 37°

steps.text: With the heights always equal, collision only needs the horizontal positions to meet; write these with A moving toward B and B moving toward A.
Set the two horizontal positions equal and solve for the collision time.
Use this time in A's own displacement equations to get the collision point P, then find its distance from A.
steps.equation: xP ≈ 56.5 m, yP = 30t − 5t² ≈ 26.7 m, PA = √(xP²+yP²) ≈ 62.5 m
steps.why_this_step: PA is the straight-line distance from A's starting point to the actual collision point, found from A's own horizontal and vertical displacement at that instant.

steps.text: Collect all three results.

final_answer.value: (a) α = 37°, (b) time of collision ≈ 1.09 s, (c) distance of collision point P from A ≈ 62.5 m

common_mistakes.text: Subtracting the horizontal components instead of adding them, using 51.96 − 40 = 11.96 m/s as the closing speed, which gives a wrong time of about 8.4 s.

question.text: At t = 0, a body is launched from a spot on a planet's surface (taken as horizontal), moving with some fixed speed at some fixed angle. As time t (in seconds) elapses, its horizontal displacement x and vertical displacement y, both in metres, follow x = (10√3)t and y = 10t − t². What is the greatest height the body reaches?
conditions: projected at t = 0 from the planet's surface
planet's surface is taken as horizontal
x = (10√3)t and y = 10t − t², x and y in metres, t in seconds

solution.approach: The maximum height is reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero, so differentiate the given vertical displacement and set it to zero.

steps.text: Differentiate the vertical displacement with respect to time to get the vertical velocity.
Set the vertical velocity to zero to find the time of maximum height.
Substitute t = 5 s back into the vertical displacement equation.

question.text: Assertion: Two objects are launched as projectiles; one climbs to a maximum height of 4H while the other climbs to a maximum height of H. For the two to land the same horizontal distance away, their horizontal velocity components need to be in a 1 : 2 ratio. Reason: A projectile's horizontal range equals its horizontal velocity component multiplied by its total time of flight.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: maximum height of the first projectile is 4H
maximum height of the second projectile is H
the two projectiles have equal horizontal ranges

solution.approach: The heights 4H and H fix the ratio of vertical launch speeds, which fixes the ratio of flight times; equal ranges then fix the ratio of horizontal launch speeds.

steps.text: Write the maximum height of each projectile in terms of its own vertical launch speed.
Divide the two height equations to get the ratio of vertical launch speeds.
Time of flight is proportional to the vertical launch speed, so this gives the ratio of the two times of flight.
Range equals the horizontal launch speed times the time of flight, and the Reason states exactly this formula; set the two ranges equal.
Substitute T₁ = 2T₂ and solve for the ratio of horizontal launch speeds.
This ratio of 1 : 2 matches the Assertion exactly, and the Reason (R = uₓ·T) is the very formula used to derive it, so both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the ratio of horizontal speeds equal to the ratio of vertical speeds instead of its reciprocal, giving 2 : 1 instead of 1 : 2.
Accepting both statements as true but treating R = uₓ×T as unrelated background information rather than the formula that proves the ratio.

question.text: A particle starts its projectile motion from the base of a ramp that is tilted at 30° to the horizontal. Find the angle α, measured from the horizontal, that the particle must be launched at so that its range measured along the ramp is as large as possible.
conditions: particle launched from the base of a 30° incline
angle sought is measured from the horizontal
range is to be maximized along the incline

solution.approach: The range up an incline is a function of the launch angle from the horizontal, and its maximum sits at a fixed angle above 45° set by the incline's slope.

steps.text: For a particle launched from the bottom of an incline of angle β, at an angle α from the horizontal, the range measured along the incline is a known function of α, β, u and g.
Maximizing R with respect to α, holding u, β and g fixed, gives a fixed relation between the best launch angle α and the incline angle β.
Substitute the given incline angle into this relation.
Add these two angles to get the launch angle that gives the maximum range up the incline.

common_mistakes.text: Using the flat-ground result of 45° for maximum range, ignoring that the incline shifts the best angle upward.
Measuring the launch angle from the incline surface instead of from the horizontal, which changes the numeric value reported.

question.text: A plane flies level at 600 km/h, cruising 1960 m above the ground. The instant it passes directly over ground point A, a package is released from it. The package touches down at point B. Work out the distance between A and B.
conditions: package is released (dropped) while the plane flies horizontally
release point is directly above ground point A
package lands on the ground at point B

A curved path leads from O down to landing point B on the ground; A and B lie on the same horizontal ground line, and the distance between them is what must be found.

solution.approach: Convert the plane's speed to SI units, find the fall time from the height using g = 9.8 m/s², then multiply to get the horizontal distance covered.

Find the time to fall the given height from rest, using g = 9.8 m/s².
The dropped body keeps the plane's horizontal velocity throughout the fall, so the horizontal distance AB equals speed times time.

question.text: A particle's motion begins with a velocity given by v = 3î + 4ĵ. A steady force, F = 4î − 3ĵ, acts on the particle throughout its motion. What shape does its trajectory take?
conditions: force acting on the particle is constant

solution.approach: Check whether the constant force is perpendicular to the initial velocity, which is the same setup as ordinary projectile motion turned sideways.

steps.text: Find the dot product of the initial velocity and the force to check if they are perpendicular.
The dot product is zero, so the constant force acts perpendicular to the initial velocity direction, at every instant, since both stay fixed vectors.
A constant force acting perpendicular to the initial velocity produces the same shape of path as a projectile launched horizontally under gravity, which is a parabola.

final_answer.value: parabolic

common_mistakes.text: Since the force is perpendicular to the velocity at the start, a student may wrongly assume circular motion; but circular motion needs the force direction to keep turning, while here it stays fixed.

question.text: For a projectile moving at low speed, its acceleration stays constant throughout the flight. Judge whether this claim is right or wrong.
conditions: projectile moves at low speed

solution.approach: Check whether the acceleration stays constant in magnitude and direction throughout the motion.

steps.text: At low speed, air resistance is negligible, so the only force on the particle is its own weight.

Since this acceleration stays fixed in both magnitude and direction throughout the flight, the motion is uniformly accelerated, even though the velocity direction keeps changing along the curved path.
So the statement is true.

final_answer.value: True. At low speed, the only acceleration acting is g, constant in magnitude and direction, so the motion is uniformly accelerated.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a curved path means the acceleration is changing, but a curved path only shows that the velocity direction changes, not the acceleration.

question.text: A ball leaves the edge of a flat tabletop standing 4 m above the ground, rolling off horizontally with no initial drop. It touches down on the ground at a spot located 5 m away, measured horizontally from the table's edge. Determine how fast the ball was travelling the moment it left the tabletop.

The ball leaves A moving horizontally (shown by an arrow v) and follows a curved path down to point C on the ground, which is 5 m horizontally from B.

solution.approach: Find the time of fall from the 4 m drop using g = 9.8 m/s² (no value given), then divide the 5 m horizontal distance by that time.

Divide the 5 m horizontal distance by this time to get the constant horizontal launch speed.

question.text: A student says that the path of a projectile is a 3-dimensional motion. Decide if this claim is correct or not.

solution.approach: Check whether the projectile's path can be contained in a single plane.

steps.text: The initial velocity and the acceleration due to gravity are two vectors; together they fix a single plane, the vertical plane containing the launch direction.
Gravity acts only within that plane, so there is no force pushing the particle out of it, and its path stays inside that one plane for the whole flight.
So the statement is false: projectile motion needs only two coordinates and is two-dimensional (planar), not three-dimensional.

final_answer.value: False. Projectile motion is two-dimensional; it occurs entirely within one vertical plane containing the initial velocity and gravity.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming any motion with a curved path in space must need all three directions, without checking that the initial velocity and gravity define only one plane.

question.text: In which specific situations can the standard equations for time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range be used directly for a projectile's motion, without any adjustment?

solution.approach: State the condition under which the range, time of flight and maximum height formulas hold, based on how they are derived.

steps.text: The formulas R = u²sin2θ/g and T = 2u sinθ/g are derived by setting the net vertical displacement to zero when the particle lands; H = u²sin²θ/(2g) is derived by setting the vertical velocity to zero at the highest point.
Setting the vertical displacement to zero at landing is correct only when the point of landing is at the same height as the point of projection.
The derivation also assumes g stays constant through the flight and that no other force, such as air resistance, changes the motion.
steps.why_this_step: A changing g or an added resistive force would change the equations of motion the formulas are built from.

steps.text: So the three formulas can be used directly only when the particle is projected from and lands on the same horizontal level, with g constant and no air resistance.

final_answer.value: The formulas apply directly only when the particle is projected from and lands on the same horizontal level, for example ground to ground, with g constant and no air resistance.

question.text: Assertion: Object A is thrown straight upward from a point on the ground. At the same instant, object B is launched from a different point on the ground and follows a curved projectile path, as pictured. Object A comes back down to the ground after 4 seconds, and at that same instant object B lands on object A. For this to happen, the peak height H reached by B works out to be 20 m. (Take g = 10 m/s².) Reason: For this situation to occur, the two objects must be launched with equal speeds.

options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

solution.approach: Particle A's flight time fixes its own launch speed; requiring B to land on A at the same instant fixes only B's vertical launch speed, not B's full speed.

steps.text: Particle A is thrown straight up and returns to the ground in 4 s, so find its launch speed from the time of flight.
Particle B collides with A at the instant A returns to the ground, so B is also in flight for 4 s.
Find the vertical component of B's launch velocity from its own time of flight, using the same relation as for A.
The maximum height of a projectile depends only on the vertical component of its launch velocity.
This confirms the Assertion: H = 20 m, and this value does not depend on B's horizontal launch speed, which the given data never fixes.
Because B's horizontal speed is unknown and generally nonzero, B's full launch speed need not equal A's 20 m/s, so the Reason is false even though the Assertion is true.

question.text: A gun sprays bullets at a fixed muzzle speed v₀ as it swings all the way around, covering the full 360° in one horizontal sweep. Find the largest ground area the bullets can land within.

every bullet leaves the muzzle at speed v₀

steps.text: Write the maximum range of a bullet fired with speed v₀, which occurs at 45° and sets the farthest distance reached in any direction.
As the gun rotates through 360°, the set of farthest points forms a circle of radius R_max.
The area covered is π times the square of this radius.

question.text: A grasshopper's longest possible jump covers 1.6 m, and it spends essentially no time resting on the ground between jumps. What horizontal distance does it cover in 10√2 s?

negligible time spent on the ground between jumps

question.text: A particle travels in the xy plane under a constant acceleration 'a' pointing along the negative y-direction. Its path is described by y = px − qx², with p and q both positive constants. Determine the particle's velocity, magnitude and direction, as it passes through the origin.
conditions: particle moves in the xy-plane
acceleration is constant, of magnitude a, directed along the negative y-axis
p and q are positive constants in the path equation y = px − qx²

solution.approach: Match the given trajectory to the standard projectile path written in terms of time, so the coefficients of x and x² give the two velocity components.

steps.text: Since the acceleration is only along −y, the horizontal velocity stays constant and the horizontal position is uₓt.
Write the vertical position using this time, with a as the acceleration magnitude and u_y the initial vertical velocity.
Compare this with the given equation term by term.
Solve the second equation for the horizontal velocity component.
Use the first equation to get the vertical velocity component, then combine the components to get the velocity's magnitude and direction at the origin.
steps.equation: u_y = p√(a/(2q)); v = √(a/(2q)) (î + p ĵ), |v| = √(a/(2q)) × √(1 + p²) = √(a(1 + p²)/(2q)), direction tan⁻¹p above the x-axis

question.text: A projectile is launched with speed 2√(gh). It just skims over two walls, each of height h, separated from each other by a distance 2h. Prove that the duration it spends traveling between the two walls equals 2√(h/g). As a method hint: first work out the speed at height h, then treat that as a fresh initial speed with 2h as the range.
conditions: particle projected so it just grazes the tops of both walls
the two walls are of equal height h
the walls are separated by a distance 2h

solution.approach: The horizontal velocity stays constant, and the speed at the wall-crossing height satisfies a mini-projectile range condition that forces the horizontal and vertical velocities there to be equal.

steps.text: The horizontal velocity component never changes during flight, so the speed at height h relates to the launch speed through the usual height-velocity equation.
Treat the point where the particle first reaches height h as a new launch point. It returns to the same height h after a horizontal distance of 2h, exactly like a projectile range.
Combine the two relations above; they force the horizontal and vertical velocities at height h to be equal.
steps.equation: vₓ² + v_y1² = 2gh and vₓv_y1 = gh ⟹ (vₓ − v_y1)² = 0 ⟹ vₓ = v_y1 = √(gh)

steps.text: The time between the walls is the flight time of the mini-projectile, which is twice the vertical velocity at height h divided by g.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full launch speed u in place of the horizontal velocity between the walls gives t = 2h/u, which is exactly half the correct time.

question.text: Assertion: Taking g = 10 m/s², the claim is that in projectile motion the particle's speed changes by 10 m/s during every second of flight. Reason: Acceleration is defined as the rate at which velocity changes.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Acceleration changes the velocity vector by a fixed amount each second, but speed is the length of that vector, which does not change by that same fixed amount.

steps.text: Take a projectile with both horizontal and vertical velocity components, and track its speed second by second.
The vertical component of velocity does change by exactly 10 m/s every second, since the vertical acceleration is constant.
The horizontal component never changes, and speed is the length of the full velocity vector, not only its vertical part.
Because speed combines both components through a square root, its change from one second to the next is not a fixed 10 m/s; it is largest near the ground and smallest near the top of the flight.

So the Assertion is false because it confuses the constant change in the velocity vector with the varying change in speed, while the Reason — that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — is a true, separate statement.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason describes the vector velocity correctly; the Assertion wrongly applies that fact to the scalar speed.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Confusing velocity with speed, so a constant 10 m/s change in the velocity vector is wrongly read as a constant 10 m/s change in speed.

Accepting the Assertion, and marking the Reason false because the student believes acceleration is defined as the rate of change of speed, so a definition worded in terms of velocity looks wrong to them.

question.text: A car starts from rest at the origin and accelerates at 2 m/s² along the positive x-axis. A man stands at the back of the car holding a gun. He fires a bullet at time t = 4 s, and this bullet meets a bird in flight at the later time t = 8 s. At that instant the bird's position vector is 40î + 80ĵ + 40k̂. Find the bullet's velocity of projection, given that the y-axis lies in the horizontal plane and g = 10 m/s².
conditions: car starts from rest at the origin
car's acceleration is 2 m/s² along the positive x-axis
bullet is fired at t = 4 s
bullet reaches the bird at t = 8 s
bird's position vector at t = 8 s is 40î + 80ĵ + 40k̂
y-axis lies in the horizontal plane
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A small illustration shows a man standing at the back of a moving car, arms outstretched, suggesting he holds a gun while the vehicle accelerates forward; no numeric values are marked on it.

solution.approach: Find the car's position when the bullet is fired, then use the bullet's projectile motion over 4 s to match the bird's given position.

steps.text: Find the car's position at t = 4 s, when the bullet is fired, since the car starts from rest at the origin.
The bullet travels from t = 4 s to t = 8 s before reaching the bird.
The x and y directions have no acceleration, so match the bird's x and y coordinates using the launch velocity components and the starting point found above.
Solve for the horizontal launch velocity components.
The z direction has acceleration −g, so match the bird's height using the vertical launch component.
Solve for the vertical launch component.
The velocity of projection is the vector with these three components, and its magnitude follows from them. This is the velocity relative to the ground.
The gun is mounted on the car, which is still accelerating, so the velocity of projection relative to the gun is the ground-frame velocity minus the car's velocity at the firing instant t = 4 s.
steps.equation: car velocity at t = 4 s = 2(4) = 8 m/s along x; v (relative to gun) = (6−8)î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ = −2î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, |v| = √(2² + 20² + 30²) = √1304 ≈ 36.1 m/s

final_answer.value: Relative to the ground: v = 6î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, magnitude 2√334 m/s ≈ 36.6 m/s. Relative to the gun (which moves with the car at 8î m/s at t = 4 s): v = −2î + 20ĵ + 30k̂ m/s, magnitude √1304 ≈ 36.1 m/s

common_mistakes.text: Measuring the bullet's motion from the origin instead of from the car's position at firing, which gives vₓ = 10 m/s and a wrong speed of 10√14 ≈ 37.4 m/s.

question.text: Show that when a projectile is launched at the angle that gives the greatest possible horizontal range, that maximum range works out to four times the greatest height it reaches.
conditions: projectile launched at the angle giving the greatest horizontal range

solution.approach: Evaluate the range and the maximum height at the angle that gives maximum range, then show one is four times the other.

steps.text: The horizontal range is maximum at 45°, so evaluate the range formula there.
Evaluate the maximum height reached at this same 45° angle.
Multiply this height by 4 and compare it with the range found above.
steps.why_this_step: Both expressions reduce to the same quantity u²/g, so the range at the angle of maximum range equals four times the height reached at that angle.

final_answer.value: At the 45° angle of maximum range, R_max = u²/g and 4H = u²/g, so R_max equals 4H.

common_mistakes.text: Using H = u²sin²45°/g in the height formula, forgetting the factor 2 in the denominator; this makes 4H = 2u²/g, twice the correct range instead of equal to it.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find how long after being launched the particle reaches the ground at point P.

tower height (O above Q) is 45 m
g = 10 m/s²
Q is the foot of the tower on the ground and P is the landing point

Q is the point directly below O at the base of the tower on the ground. The particle follows a curved path from O and lands at point P on the ground, to the right of Q.

solution.approach: Horizontal projectile from height 45 m; find the fall time from the height, then use it for the horizontal distance and the two velocity components at landing.

steps.text: Write the height fallen as a function of time for a horizontal launch, using g = 10 m/s².
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
Find the horizontal distance QP, since the horizontal velocity stays constant (part b).
Find the horizontal and vertical velocity components at P.
Combine the components to get the speed and direction at P: the magnitude is the hypotenuse of the 40 m/s and 30 m/s components, and the direction is the angle whose tangent is 30/40.
steps.equation: (a) t = 3 s (b) QP = 120 m (c) v = √(40² + 30²) = 50 m/s at 37° below the horizontal

final_answer.value: (a) t = 3 s, (b) QP = 120 m, (c) v = 50 m/s at 37° below the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Adding the horizontal and vertical speeds directly instead of combining them as vectors, giving 40 + 30 = 70 m/s instead of 50 m/s.

question.text: A particle leaves the ground with launch speed 40 m/s, directed 60° from the horizontal.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the particle's speed at the instant its velocity direction makes 37° with the horizontal.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the time (or times) at which this occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: At that same instant, find how high up (vertical height) and how far out (horizontal distance) the particle is, measured from where it started. Use g = 10 m/s².

conditions: particle launched from ground level
launch speed 40 m/s at 60° from the horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: The particle's parabolic path starts at the origin at 60° above the horizontal with speed 40 m/s. On the way up, at time t₁, its velocity vector makes 37° with the horizontal, with vertical rise h and horizontal distance x₁ marked at that point. On the way down, at a later time t₂, the velocity vector again makes 37° with the horizontal, with the same rise h now on the descending side and horizontal distance x₂ marked.

solution.approach: Use the constant horizontal component with the 37° angle to get the speed, then find the two times and the common height and distances at those instants.

steps.text: Resolve the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical parts; the horizontal part stays constant throughout the flight.
At the instant the velocity makes 37° with the horizontal, the horizontal component still equals ux, so the speed follows from v = ux/cos37°.
Find the two times this 37° angle occurs, once rising (vy positive) and once falling (vy negative), from vy = uy − gt.
Since the vertical speed has the same size (15 m/s) at both instants, both are at the same height; find that height and the two horizontal distances.
Collect all three results.

final_answer.value: (a) speed = 25 m/s at both instants, (b) t₁ ≈ 1.96 s (rising) and t₂ ≈ 4.96 s (falling), (c) height ≈ 48.75 m at both instants; horizontal distance ≈ 39.3 m at t₁ and ≈ 99.3 m at t₂

common_mistakes.text: Finding the speed as v = ux/sin37° = 20/0.6 ≈ 33.3 m/s, mixing up sine and cosine when relating the horizontal component to the resultant speed.

question.text: Two stones leave the ground at the same initial speed but at two different angles above the horizontal, and they both travel the same horizontal range. One of the stones is fired at π/3 and climbs to a peak height of 102 m. Find the peak height reached by the second stone, in metres.
conditions: both stones launched with the same initial speed
the two stones have equal horizontal ranges
first stone launched at π/3 to the horizontal

solution.approach: Equal range at the same speed means the two angles are complementary, so find the second angle and scale the given maximum height by the ratio of sine squares.

steps.text: For the same speed, two angles give the same range only if they are complementary, so the second angle is 90° − 60° = 30°.
Write the maximum height formula for both angles at the same speed u.
Divide the height at 30° by the height at 60°; the u² and 2g cancel.
Multiply the given height by this ratio to get the second height.

common_mistakes.text: Inverting the ratio, dividing the 60° height's sine-square term by the 30° height's sine-square term instead, gives 306 m, which is not among the printed options.

question.text: Using the launch data marked in the diagram, work out how long the projectile stays in the air and how far it travels along the slanted surface, taking g = 10 m/s².
conditions: incline at 30° to the horizontal
launch speed 20√2 m/s at 45° to the horizontal
g = 10 m/s²
the projectile lands on the incline

figure.description: An inclined plane rises to the right from a point on level ground at 30° to the horizontal. From that same point a projectile is launched at 20√2 m/s, its velocity making 45° with the horizontal, so that it is steeper than the incline by 15° and lands on the incline.

solution.approach: Resolve the velocity and gravity along and perpendicular to the incline; the projectile lands on the incline when the perpendicular displacement returns to zero.

steps.text: In the figure the velocity is drawn steeper than the incline. It makes 45° with the horizontal while the incline makes 30° with the horizontal, both measured from the same point at the base of the incline. So the velocity makes 45° minus 30° with the incline surface, and the projectile lands further up the slope.
steps.why_this_step: The angle between the velocity and the incline surface, not the angle with the horizontal, decides the motion along the incline.

steps.text: Take axes along the incline and perpendicular to it. Resolve the initial velocity into these two directions, and resolve gravity the same way.
steps.equation: along incline: u cos15° ; perpendicular: u sin15° ; g along incline: g sin30° ; g perpendicular: g cos30°

steps.text: The projectile returns to the incline surface when the perpendicular displacement becomes zero again. This gives the time of flight.
Range along the incline is the along-incline distance covered in time T, using the along-incline part of gravity that slows the climb.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the incline and using the flat-ground formulas T = 2u sinθ/g and R = u² sin2θ/g gives T = 4 s and R = 80 m, missing that the ground here is sloped.
Using the angle sum 45°+30° instead of the difference 45°−30° gives T ≈ 6.31 s and R ≈ 145.71 m, which is the answer for the projectile fired down the incline, not up it.

conditions: projected from ground level
initial speed 20√2 m/s
launch angle 45° above horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Write the height above ground as a function of time and solve for the times at which it equals 15 m.

steps.text: Find the vertical component of the launch velocity.
Write the height as a function of time.
Set the height equal to 15 m and simplify to a quadratic.
Factor the quadratic to find both times the particle is at this height.
